item.title: Garcia Richard Wins DPNM SCC Special Selection, Joins Haaland on Democratic Ticket for Lieutenant Governor
item.description:
SANTA FE, N.M. — State Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard won a special election held Thursday by the Democratic Party of New Mexico's State Central Committee, securing the party's nomination for lieutenant governor and joining Deb Haaland atop the Democratic ticket ahead of the November general election.

Garcia Richard replaces Maggie Toulouse Oliver on the ballot. The committee's selection followed a competitive race against state Sen. Harold Pope, whom Garcia Richard thanked afterward for what she called a spirited campaign and for his ongoing service to New Mexicans.

Garcia Richard, a former public school teacher, served in the New Mexico House of Representatives before her election as Commissioner of Public Lands, a role she has held for two terms. In the House, she worked on legislation that helped establish the state's universal childcare program. As land commissioner, her office reports generating more than $15 billion in state funding for public education, along with job growth tied to clean energy development and a series of environmental protections for the state's air, land and water.

"I am deeply humbled and honored to earn the trust of the DPNM State Central Committee and to join Deb Haaland on this ticket," Garcia Richard said in a statement. "New Mexicans work incredibly hard, and they deserve a government that works just as hard for them. From my time in the classroom to the State House and the State Land Office, I have never stopped fighting for our communities. Deb and I share a vision for a New Mexico where we lower costs, increase access to healthcare, build safer communities, and provide a world-class public education for every child."

With the ticket now finalized, the Haaland-Garcia Richard campaign is turning its attention to the general election. Garcia Richard framed the contest as a choice between competing visions for the state's direction.

"The stakes this November could not be higher," Garcia Richard said. "While our Republican opponents want to drag our state backward with extreme, out-of-touch policies that will hurt working families and drive up costs, Deb Haaland and I are looking toward a brighter future. Our message is clear: we are helping kids read earlier and bringing trades back to schools in a big way, creating more affordable and accessible healthcare, getting illegal drugs off our streets, and making life more affordable with tax breaks to working people, universal childcare, and cheaper housing costs. We are ready to take our message to every corner of New Mexico and build a winning coalition that will deliver on our promises to the people."

Locally in Otero County the local Democratic Party via acting chair Joy Bordenave said, " we are thrilled the selection process is now completed and we can move forward with getting both Deb and Stephanie elected via this historic ticket. Locally, we will be working hard to get out the vote for these candidates as well as those Democats and Independents up and down the ballot." 

The Haaland-Garcia Richard ticket will face its Republican opponents Gregg Hull (for governor) and David Gallegos (for lieutenant governor) on the November ballot.

item.title: Alamogordo City Commission Approves Budget, $109 Million Cash on Hand
item.description:
Finance Authority Report Shows Strong Cash Position as FY2026 Reaches Midpoint

The City of Alamogordo’s Commission met on July 30 to officially approve Resolution 2026-28, ratifying the city’s financial position through the end of the second quarter of fiscal year 2026. The action marks the required regulatory approval of financial figures as of June 30, 2026.

According to the Finance Authority Quarterly Report presented by Finance Director Evelyn Huff, the city maintains a robust financial position with combined cash and investments totaling $109.8 million.

Strong Revenue Collections

The first half of the fiscal year has generated encouraging financial results. The city collected $98.5 million in revenues against expenditures of $86.5 million, contributing to a year-to-date surplus position.

“These numbers demonstrate solid financial management and revenue collection efforts across all city departments,” Huff noted in the report.

Key Financial Metrics

• Beginning Cash Balance: $7.48 million

• Revenues (YTD): $98.47 million

• Expenditures (YTD): $86.46 million

• Investments: $90.62 million

• Ending Cash Plus Investments: $109.81 million

The city also processed $26.55 million in inter-fund transfers during the period, reflecting routine operational allocation of resources across municipal departments.

State Compliance and Next Steps

The approval satisfies state regulatory requirements mandating City Commission authorization of quarterly financial reports. Finance Director Huff indicated that the finalized numbers will be uploaded to the state’s Local Government Budget System (LGBMS) prior to the July 31, 2026 deadline.

“This approval ensures our compliance with state requirements and provides transparency to our residents about the city’s financial health,” a city official stated.

The Commission proceeded with the action despite the absence of Commissioners Baxter Patillo and Stephen Burnett. The Mayor McDonald and four additional commissioners were present, establishing the required quorum for official action.

Looking Ahead

With six months of the fiscal year complete, city officials are positioned to conduct year-to-date budget analysis comparing actual revenues and expenditures to budgeted projections. This data will inform final quarter planning and any necessary adjustments to departmental spending as FY2026 concludes.

The full year-to-date budget report comparing actual to projected figures is available through the City Finance Department.

Oh good.  Maybe we could get some roads fixed now?  Or at least some nearly invisible lane lines repainted?  🙄

item.title: Otero County Approves Raises for Staff and Elected Officials
item.description:
The Otero County Commission’s approval of the FY2027 budget on July 30, 2026 highlighted a critical but often misunderstood aspect of county government: the distinct roles and responsibilities of two separate financial leadership positions that work in tandem to manage public funds.

As Karl Melton assumes his position as Otero County Treasurer—an elected position—and the Finance Department continues its oversight of daily operations and budget compliance, understanding this dual structure is essential to comprehending how counties manage taxpayer resources.

The Treasurer’s Role: Cash Management and Investments

The county treasurer serves as the property tax collector and investment officer for public funds in Otero County. This elected position, which carries a four-year term limited to two terms, carries specific and narrowly defined responsibilities focused on cash flow and investment strategy.

To understand the distinction listen to Karl Melton on Alamogordo Town News streaming via KALHRadio.org

https://www.youtube.com/live/tbwcASsVwRY?is=TviPizTF3q1UBsnV

Karl Melton, who took office in January 2026 after winning the November 2024 election, manages the county’s liquid assets and investment portfolio. Upon taking office, Melton stated that “we will immediately work on increasing the transparency of county investments, improving the investment portfolio to increase returns, and generating more revenue for the county’s budget.”

The treasurer’s authority is circumscribed by law and regulation. Importantly, the treasurer does not make decisions on the allocation of funds nor sets policy on tax spending. Instead, the treasurer operates within parameters set by statute, county policy, and the commission’s budget directives.

The Otero County Finance Department: Operations and Compliance

In contrast, the Finance Department—headed by a director appointed by the county—manages the daily operational side of the budget. This includes expenditure tracking, revenue projections, fund allocation to departments, budget performance analysis, and ensuring compliance with county financial policies and state regulations.

The Finance Director presented the FY2027 budget to the commission, detailed year-to-date budget reports, discussed revenue projections, and made recommendations on fund allocation and department spending. This individual works closely with department heads to ensure spending aligns with approved budgets and identifies variations between projected and actual expenditures.

How They Work Together

The relationship between these two offices is complementary but separate:

• Treasurer’s Office: Safeguards cash reserves, manages investments in bonds and securities, ensures funds are invested in compliance with county investment policy, collects property taxes, and pursues tax collection strategies

• Finance Department: Allocates those available funds to departments, tracks spending against budget, projects revenues and expenditures, identifies budget variances, and ensures regulatory compliance

Together, they create a system of checks and balances where one office manages the county’s money while the other determines how it’s spent—with the County Commission serving as the body that sets overall financial policy and approves the budget framework.

FY2027 Budget Approval Reflects Dual Structure

The county’s approval of its FY2027 budget reflected this dual responsibility. The Finance Director presented detailed spending plans, revenue projections, and departmental allocations. The commission discussed and approved these operational parameters. Meanwhile, the Treasurer’s Office—under Melton’s leadership—will manage the actual cash positions, investments, and liquidity necessary to support those operations.

The budget includes a projected General Fund ending cash balance of $1.8 million, with a mandatory three-month reserve of $6.6 million dictated by law. The Treasurer’s Office will be responsible for managing those reserve levels and ensuring compliance with investment policies. The Finance Department will track whether actual expenditures align with the approved budget allocation.

The slightly better then expected financial picture for the county enabled commissioners to approve a $1.50 per hour across-the-board pay increase for all county employees and elected officials—something that appeared impossible at the beginning of the fiscal year.
“We have some extra money coming in, and if we’re gonna do it, it would be a good time to do it,” commissioners stated, emphasizing both the improved financial position and the practical necessity of competitive compensation to retain skilled employees.
The county also approved funding for three new positions: two part-time animal shelter assistants, two transfer station attendants, and one legal department custodian to address overwhelming documentation workload.

However, the county’s budget reveals a financially constrained operation. The General Fund is projected to maintain only $1.8 million in ending cash balance—a figure that becomes even tighter when accounting for the mandatory $6.6 million three-month reserve requirement mandated by state law. The Road Fund, similarly operating under a one-month reserve requirement, is projected to end the year with essentially zero dollars.

Contrasting Narratives: County vs. City Financial Reporting

The structural difference between the treasurer and finance roles reflects a broader distinction in how county and city governments present their financial pictures to the public—a difference evident in how Otero County and the City of Alamogordo reported their respective budgets on the same day.

The City of Alamogordo’s financial reporting emphasizes detailed numerical documentation. The city provided “a recap summary of all funds, showing beginning cash, revenues, transfers, expenditures, investments and ending cash,” along with “a year-to-date budget report for the period ending June 30, 2026” that “illustrates how the actual revenues and expenditures compare to the budgeted amounts.” The city’s approach relies on comprehensive data presentation and comparative analysis.

Otero County’s budget approval, by contrast, employed a more narrative and discussion-based approach. Finance Director presented the budget verbally to the commission, emphasizing that revenues “ended up being a bit more than I had expected” and highlighting specific policy decisions such as allocating subsidized funds “to the penny” of what they need. The county commission engaged in extended dialogue about the implications of budget positions, employee compensation needs, and strategic priorities.

The city’s approach—detailed financial tables, comparative budget analysis, and numerical precision—reflects a government managing substantially larger revenues ($98.5 million in half-year revenues) and maintaining significantly larger reserves ($109.8 million in combined cash and investments).

The county’s more narrative approach—discussion of revenue surprises, strategic budget allocation decisions, and qualitative assessment—reflects an organization operating with tighter margins where every dollar allocation carries greater significance. With a General Fund of only $1.8 million in ending balance before mandatory reserves, the county’s finance leadership must discuss trade-offs and strategic choices in ways a larger government need not.

Conclusion

The distinction between Otero County’s Treasurer and Finance Department reflects a fundamental principle of governmental financial management: separation of custody from allocation. The Treasurer safeguards and invests public money; the Finance Department directs its use. This division protects taxpayers by ensuring no single official can both determine spending priorities and control the funds implementing those priorities.

However, the contrasting narratives between county and city reporting reveal a deeper truth about scale and financial resilience.

When a government operates with substantial reserves and predictable revenues, it can afford detailed numerical reporting and comparative analysis.

When a government operates closer to its financial limits, as Otero County does, the emphasis shifts to strategic narrative—explaining why this year revenues exceeded expectations, why certain departments received only what they absolutely need, and why employee compensation became possible only through disciplined budget management.

Both approaches serve a level of transparency with the city providing line by line transparency in discussions with the public, but they reflect different financial realities. The county encourages citizens to call the finance director or the treasurer for transparency. Mr Melton the County Treasurer, in an earlier interview encouraged citizen engagement, Otero County finance less so.

The City of Alamogordo can present the numbers and let them speak due to their level of transparency and a city focused on building a sound budget via Dr Hernandez’s tenure as City Manager. Mr Stockwell inherited a city in a strong financial position. The county by contrast in recent years has struggled with audit results and tight budgets with little wiggle room.

Otero County must explain the story behind the numbers to help stakeholders understand how limited resources are allocated strategically for maximum benefit to county residents the contrast in positions and leadership is glaring.

item.title: Alamogordo Police Department Activity Summary: July 20-26, 2026
item.description:
The Alamogordo Police Department handled a diverse array of criminal activity and public safety issues during the week of July 20-26, 2026, reflecting a typical range of urban law enforcement challenges. The department's weekly activity logs document arrests, citations, and investigations spanning drug trafficking, assault, theft, traffic violations, and disorderly conduct.

According to the police department's official records, the week began with multiple arrests related to drug enforcement operations. Officers working with the White Mountain Drug Task Force made significant arrests on controlled substance charges, with several individuals charged with trafficking and possession offenses. These cases resulted in incarcerations at the Otero County Detention Center pending court proceedings, as the department continues its ongoing efforts to combat drug-related crime in the community.

Domestic violence and assault cases also featured prominently in the week's reports. Multiple incidents involving battery against household members were documented, along with assault investigations and related criminal damage to property charges. The police department reminds residents that domestic violence is a serious crime with significant legal consequences, and those experiencing abuse are encouraged to contact law enforcement.

"This does not include all calls for service the Alamogordo Police Department responded to during this time frame," according to the department's weekly activity log documentation. The summary focuses on major criminal activities and arrests but represents only a portion of the department's total workload.

Traffic enforcement yielded multiple citations and arrests. One individual was arrested on a DUI charge following a traffic stop and was released on recognizance with a scheduled court date. Additionally, officers cited multiple drivers for failure to appear on existing warrants, and one vehicle-related fraud case resulted in a Municipal Court summons for an individual accused of selling a vehicle without transferring ownership.

Retail theft continued to plague local businesses during the week. Three separate shoplifting investigations at Alamogordo retailers resulted in citations and arrests. One incident involved a juvenile referred to Juvenile Probation Officer custody, underscoring concerns about youth involvement in criminal activity. Police encourage business owners to remain vigilant and report suspected theft to law enforcement.

Public disturbance incidents concentrated in the 8th Street and downtown areas resulted in multiple citations and arrests for disorderly conduct and public affray. One juvenile male was referred to Juvenile Probation Officer custody following a disturbance incident. The police department emphasizes that disorderly conduct charges can result in fines and potential jail time.

The week also included several arrests on outstanding warrants. Individuals arrested on Municipal and Magistrate Court warrants for failure to appear in court were either incarcerated pending court appearances or released on their own recognizance with scheduled court dates. These cases reflect the ongoing challenge of ensuring compliance with court orders.

Additional incidents handled by the department included citations for trespassing, aggravated indecent exposure charges with multiple related offenses, animal control violations, and park closure hour violations. One incident involved charges of indecent exposure with additional related charges pending court appearances.

The Alamogordo Police Department operates under a community policing model, balancing enforcement with community engagement. The department encourages residents with information about criminal activity to contact the police or submit anonymous tips. For non-emergency reporting, residents can call 575-439-4300.

Residents seeking detailed information about any of these incidents can request full reports through the city website or by contacting the Police Department Records Division during business hours, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The complete weekly activity logs are available through the City of Alamogordo Police Department at

www.ci.alamogordo.nm.us/DocumentCenter/View/18258/July-20-to-July-26-2026-PDF

For emergencies, residents should always dial 911.

Hours: Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–5 p.m.

Address: 700 Virginia Avenue, Alamogordo, NM 88310

Emergency: 911

Full Police Activity Logs: www.ci.alamogordo.nm.us (Request a Report)

item.title: SAVE THE DATE: Voices of Alamogordo Community Forum to Discuss Alamo City Dream Center Tuesday, Aug 4th, at 6 PM
item.description:
Educational and Transparency Forum Examines a Potential Community Response to Homelessness and Food Insecurity

ALAMOGORDO – As part of the ongoing 'Voices of Alamogordo' learning series, journalist Chris Edwards will host a comprehensive community forum on Tuesday, August 4th, 2026 at 6:00 PM at Otero Arts to explore the Alamo City Dream Center initiative. The forum will be streamed live on KALHRadio, YouTube, and multiple affiliate platforms for transparency and public education.

About the 'Voices of Alamogordo' Series

The 'Voices of Alamogordo' learning series is an educational initiative designed to provide Alamogordo residents with transparent, in-depth discussions on community challenges and solutions. Hosted by journalist Chris Edwards, the series brings together local leaders, advocates, and stakeholders to address critical issues facing our city. By making these conversations accessible through live streaming on KALHRadio.org, KALH Radio YouTube, and affiliate platforms, the series ensures all community members can participate in and learn about key initiatives shaping Alamogordo's future.

August 4th Forum: Understanding the Proposed Alamo City Dream Center

This edition of 'Voices of Alamogordo' will examine the proposed Alamo City Dream Center—a major community initiative aimed at addressing homelessness, food insecurity, and crisis support in Otero County. The forum will feature an expert panel discussion exploring the Dream Center's mission, operational model, and role within the broader community.

Featured Panelists

Panelists include:

● Pastor Anthony Torres and Sasha Torres, Mountain View Church (Initiative Leadership)

● Wendy Urquiedez, Community Volunteer and Affordable Housing Advocate

● Nadia Sykes, Community Partner & Housing Advocate

● Mayor Sharon McDonald, City of Alamogordo

What is the Alamo City Dream Center?

The Alamo City Dream Center is a proposed community-based social services facility proposed to be designed to serve vulnerable populations in Alamogordo and Otero County. Operating Monday through Friday from 11 AM to 8 PM, the Dream Center proposes to provide:

● Daily hot meals through an on-site soup kitchen

● Safe daytime shelter with shower and laundry facilities

● Emergency crisis relief services to Otero County residents

● Support services focused on restoring dignity and hope

● Rehab support services 

The initiative operates as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit entity with Mountain View Church providing foundational leadership and oversight. The project as proposed represents a $1.98 million capital investment and approximately 6,500 square feet of dedicated facility space. The City of Alamogordo has committed $200,000 of seed money when paired with matching grants. 

Forum Topics and Learning Objectives

During the August 4th forum at 6 pm at Otero Arts, participants will have the opportunity to:

● Learn about the Dream Center's comprehensive mission and services

● Understand the operational structure and staffing model

● Review preliminary architectural designs for the facility

● Engage directly with panelists through live question-and-answer

● Explore affordable housing and community support advocacy

● Discover volunteer and community involvement opportunities

How to Participate

Event Details:

Date: Tuesday, August 4th, 2026

Time: 6:00 PM

Location: Otero Arts, Alamogordo, NM

Attendance: Free and open to the public

Community members are welcome to attend in person. All interested residents are encouraged to participate in this important community conversation.

Live Streaming Access

For those unable to attend in person, the forum will be streamed live on the following platforms:

● KALHRadio

● YouTube (Voices of Alamogordo Live on KALH Radio)

● Multiple affiliate platforms

Commitment to Transparency and Education

The 'Voices of Alamogordo' series reflects the community's commitment to transparent, collaborative problem-solving on critical social issues. By hosting forums like this one, journalist Chris Edwards and community partners ensure that all Alamogordo residents have access to detailed, factual information about initiatives that affect their community.

About Mountain View Church and the Initiative

Mountain View Church has long served the Alamogordo community with a mission centered on compassion, support, and dignity for all residents. The Alamo City Dream Center represents a concrete expression of this mission, addressing two of the most pressing challenges facing Otero County: homelessness and food insecurity.

item.title: In Memory of Marian J. “Toto” VanWinkle
item.description:
Marian J. “Toto” VanWinkle, of Alamogordo, NM, passed away peacefully on July 25, 2026, at the age of 84, surrounded by the love of her family. She was welcomed into Heaven and reunited with the love of her life, Pete, and oldest daughter, Cindy Kay.

Marian was born September 5, 1941, to AC and Margaret Miller in Carlsbad, NM. She attended school in Weed where she graduated in 1959. She met the love of her life, Pete, on October 5, 1957, at Hillbilly Heaven and as Toto always said, “the rest was history”. They married on June 20, 1959, in Loving, NM. They started their life here in Alamogordo, NM, living in both Albuquerque and Ruidoso some time, making the full circle back to Alamogordo again in 2007. During that time, they had three children, Cindy, Craig and Kimberly.

Marian worked side by side with Pete when he was a plumbing and heating contractor while they lived in Ruidoso, NM where they later retired in 2000. She was always up for a good hunting or fishing trip, and let’s be honest, she did both better than most of us. Marian found her greatest joy in being a homemaker. She lovingly devoted her life to caring for her children, creating a home filled with warmth, faith, and unconditional love. As the years passed, nothing brought her more happiness than watching her grandchildren and great grandchildren grow, celebrating each of their milestones and cherishing every moment spent together. She was a gifted seamstress whose hands could create beautiful things, but her favorite place was always the kitchen. Whether she was preparing a family meal, baking something sweet, or preserving their own harvest through canning, Marian expressed her love through the food she made. Her kitchen was the heart of her home-a place where family gathered, stories were shared, and countless treasured memories were made.

Marian is survived by her two children, Craig (Sherry) and Kimberly; her best friend, Cecilia Price; her five grandsons, Raif (Shana), Cory (Jaclyn), Chance (Brandi), Tyler (Ashley), and Jayton. She was blessed with 6 great grandchildren, Warrick, Shaeleigh, Hayden, Arya, Claira, and Dixie; numerous cousins, nieces and nephews.

She was preceded in death by her parents, AC and Margaret Miller; her husband, Willam A. “Pete” VanWinkle; her oldest daughter, Cindy Kay Nowell; her two sisters and brother, Jeanie, Jody and Jim.

The love Pete and Marian shared throughout their 63 years of marriage was an inspiration to everyone who knew them. Together they built a life rooted in faith, family, hard work, and unwavering devotion to one another. They often reminded those around them, “Don’t grieve for what you don’t have; be thankful for what you have been given.” Their example of love, gratitude, and commitment will inspire and live on through the family they cherished most.

A memorial service will be held on August 5, 2026, at 10:00 am, at Alamogordo Funeral Home in Alamogordo, NM with Bob VanWinkle officiating. A small reception will take place following the service at Scenic Chapel in Alamogordo, NM.

In lieu of flowers, the family requests you donate to your favorite charity.

item.title: History Comes to Life: Tularosa Basin Museum Hosts “Night at the Museum” Community Event July 31st
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, NM — The Tularosa Basin Museum of History is hosting “Night at the Museum” on July 31, 2026, from 6:00 PM to 10:00 PM, marking another chapter in the institution’s growing legacy as a premier research destination in southern New Mexico dedicated to community engagement and cultural preservation.

A Gateway to the Past, Open to All

Located at 1004 N. White Sands Boulevard in Alamogordo, the museum was established in 1970 and is owned and operated by the Tularosa Basin Historical Society. Housed in an incredible Pueblo Revival building, its exhibits range from prehistoric times to the Space Race, offering visitors a comprehensive journey through the region’s defining eras and transformative moments.

Tonight’s special evening programming exemplifies the museum’s mission to make history accessible and engaging for all ages. The institution is dedicated to the preservation of local history through exhibits, educational programs, and resources highlighting the cultural heritage of the Tularosa Basin area.

A Comprehensive Collection Spanning Centuries

The museum’s collection is remarkably diverse, reflecting the complexity and richness of the region’s past. The museum holds a bison trophy head, a collection of pottery from the La Luz Pottery Factory, and artifacts from prehistoric Native American tribes that were found in caves above Alamogordo. The collection includes over 3,000 historical photographs of the local area and an archive of historical documents, plus a small interactive theatre showcasing history with films created by area students.

Among the museum’s most prized possessions, a 47-star U.S. flag stands as the prize item in the collection. Meanwhile, the museum showcases various artifacts such as coveralls worn by the only scientist to walk on the moon and the Daisy Track used for testing acceleration effects, as well as the Sonic Wind rocket sled that made history as the Fastest Man on Earth.

Visitors can learn about the early Native Americans who lived in the area, White Sands National Park, the local railroad, La Luz pottery, ranching, scouting and more, viewing artifacts and stories from the days of early man to Alamogordo’s role in the atomic and space ages.

Recent Exhibitions Celebrate Untold Stories

The museum has recently expanded its exhibition scope to encompass narratives previously underrepresented in mainstream historical discourse. The Tularosa Basin Museum of History unveiled a powerful new exhibit titled “Black History in the Basin,” which shines a long-overdue spotlight on the Black families who helped shape Alamogordo and the surrounding region. This exhibit was curated by local historians and community leaders Joe and Debra Lewandowski.

Joe Lewandowski challenged long-held misconceptions about the region’s history—particularly the legacy of the Buffalo Soldiers and the migration patterns of Black families to Alamogordo, noting that “Many of Alamogordo’s Black families arrived here through employment opportunities in the railroad and lumber industries”.

As the museum continues its mission to tell the full story of the Tularosa Basin, Black History in the Basin stands as a testament to the power of truth, representation, and community memory

Special Programs Enhance Community Connection

Beyond its permanent and rotating exhibitions, the museum serves as a cultural hub for education and engagement. The museum is open 10 am to 4 pm Monday through Saturday and offers tours of the La Luz Pottery Factory on Saturday mornings.

The La Luz Pottery Factory, a 235-acre property in La Luz, New Mexico, was built in 1930 by wealthy New England industrialist Roland Hazard and created over 90 styles of pottery that were actively collected around the world before closing in 1949. Many of the original buildings remain intact, and tours of the property are available through the Tularosa Basin Museum of History on Saturday mornings.

The museum is the base of operations for the Tularosa Basin Historic Society, which is instrumental in refurbishing the Dudley School, an important project that will showcase the authentic celebration of history, art and culture of the Hispanic community within the area.

Tonight’s Event: What to Expect

Tonight’s “Night at the Museum” continues a tradition of special evening programming designed to make the museum experience fresh and engaging for both longtime supporters and first-time visitors. Past similar events have featured ice cream socials priced at $2 per person or $5 per family, book sales featuring local history titles and rare finds, and interactive scavenger hunts that invite visitors to explore exhibits in an engaging way, with free admission to all events and welcoming all ages.

The evening format allows visitors to explore a diverse collection of exhibits that highlight the region’s history, including artifacts from Native American cultures, early settlers, and military history related to White Sands Missile Range. Visitors can explore photographs, documents, and installations that narrate the story of the basin’s development and its significance in New Mexico’s history.

Community Engagement and Support

The Tularosa Basin Museum of History is well-regarded for its comprehensive collection and enthusiastic, knowledgeable volunteer staff, with many reviewers emphasizing the museum’s ability to cover a broad range of local history within a relatively small space, including geology, Native American history, westward expansion, local culture, and military contributions to the region.

The Tularosa Basin Historical Society & Museum operates as a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization and relies on community support, membership dues, donations, and special events to sustain its mission. Tonight’s event represents both an opportunity for residents to enjoy a unique evening of historical discovery and a chance to support the institution’s ongoing preservation efforts.

Location and Accessibility

The museum benefits from public transit access with a Z-Trans stop across the street, making it easily accessible to residents throughout Alamogordo. The venue’s location in the downtown cultural arts and history district positions it as a centerpiece of Alamogordo’s commitment to preserving and celebrating local heritage.

Looking Forward

As Alamogordo continues to evolve as a modern community, institutions like the Tularosa Basin Museum of History serve a critical function in maintaining connection to the region’s past. Through efforts to tell the full story of the Tularosa Basin and welcome new voices into that narrative, the museum demonstrates the power of truth, representation, and community memory.

Join the Celebration

Tonight’s “Night at the Museum” runs from 6:00 PM to 10:00 PM at 1004 N. White Sands Boulevard, Alamogordo, NM 88310. Whether you’re a history enthusiast, a lifelong Alamogordo resident, a curious visitor, or simply seeking a meaningful evening activity, the museum invites you to step into the fascinating world of the Tularosa Basin.

For more information about tonight’s event or regular museum hours and programs, contact the Tularosa Basin Historical Society at (575) 434-4438 or visit their website at tbhsmuseum.org.

item.title: Alamo Senior Center Celebrates Vital Services and Summer Wellness
item.description:
Community Programs Thrive as Center Recognizes Staff and Volunteers; Expands Resources for Homebound Residents

The Alamo Senior Center continues to be a cornerstone of wellness and community connection for Alamogordo’s older residents, with Manager Magdalena highlighting the tremendous work behind the scenes in August’s edition of The Sentinel.

At the heart of the center’s mission is the Home-Delivered Meal program, which shows no signs of slowing down. Each weekday, coordinators, meal preparers, and dedicated volunteers work together to deliver more than 150 nutritious meals to homebound seniors throughout our community.

“This program is a true team effort,” Magdalena noted in her message to the community. “From those who coordinate and prepare meals to the dedicated volunteers who deliver them, your compassion, commitment, and generosity make a meaningful difference in the lives of our community’s seniors.”

The Numbers Tell the Story

June’s nutrition report underscores the program’s reach. In just 22 days of service, the center served 7,736 total meals—4,130 at the facility itself and 3,606 delivered to homebound seniors. Those low donation averages of $11.66 for congregate meals and $1.11 for home-delivered options reflect the center’s commitment to keeping services accessible for everyone.

Meals arrive between 10:30 a.m. and 1:00 p.m., and the center asks that clients cancel when they won’t be home—a small courtesy that ensures resources reach those who truly need them.

Beat the Heat: Safety Tips for August

As temperatures climb, the Alamo Senior Center is reminding residents to look out for one another. A phone call or visit to an elderly neighbor can make all the difference during hot summer months.

The center has released detailed hydration guidance for the season. Watch for dehydration symptoms including fatigue, headaches, muscle cramps, dizziness, and sleepiness. The key is sipping water consistently throughout the day rather than chugging large amounts at once.

High-water foods like melon, cucumber, berries, and leafy greens offer an extra boost during hot weather. Those staying active should carry water bottles, take breaks in the shade, and plan strenuous activities for cooler hours.

A Full Calendar of Activities

If you or someone you know is 60 and older, the Alamo Senior Center offers far more than meals. item.title: Pattern of Suppression: How New Mexico Government Officials Are Using Courts to Silence Citizens—and Losing
item.description:
From Santa Fe to Lea and Eddy Counties, Citizens Are Fighting Back Against Unconstitutional Restraints on Free Speech and IPRA Violations

Across the state, a clear pattern emerges: Government officials are threatening to weaponize the courts to silence criticism and block public records. But citizens and courts are fighting back and winning at every turn. Government officials be on notice. 

When a County Director Files a Restraining Order Against a Critic

On July 24, 2026, Judge Kathleen McGarry Ellenwood made a stark ruling: A Rio Arriba County Health and Human Services Director's attempt to silence a citizen through a restraining order was unconstitutional.

Ahmed Dadzie had filed suit against Cynthia Lentini for posting criticism of his official conduct on social media. Lentini, a community activist and Facebook group administrator, had commented publicly about how Dadzie ran his department. Dadzie wanted to silence her.

The judge was unequivocal: The restraining order "constitutes a prior restraint of speech in violation of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article II, Section 17 of the New Mexico Constitution."

As a public official, Dadzie bore a higher burden of proof. He failed to meet it. The evidence was "speculative, and much of it is not tied to Mr. Dadzie." The court determined that "Ms. Lentini was [not] responsible for actionable content regarding Mr. Dadzie."

But the cost to Lentini was already paid: thousands of dollars in legal fees, weeks of her life, defending constitutional rights that should never have been questioned. She filed a formal complaint with Rio Arriba County Manager Jeremy G. Maestas: "If a county employee can file an unconstitutional restraining order against a citizen for speaking about matters of public concern, then every resident should be concerned."

Maestas announced an independent investigation into Dadzie. The message was delivered: Use the courts to suppress criticism and you face investigation—and potentially your job.

The Pattern Escalates: Eddy County and the IPRA Battle

In Eddy County, the conflict reveals how government resistance to transparency cascades into years of expensive litigation.

Jason Sanchez, an Eddy County resident, filed IPRA requests seeking personnel files for deputies Jared Rostro and Eric Threlkeld. Sanchez believed the officers had mishandled his domestic custody case. The county released the files in response to his IPRA request.

Sanchez then posted screenshots of those personnel documents on Facebook under "Eddy County Wall of Shame," arguing they demonstrated a pattern of officer misconduct. He used the information to support his own lawsuit against the deputies for wrongful prosecution.

The deputies responded in January 2024 by suing both Eddy County and Sanchez in federal court, alleging wrongful disclosure under IPRA and invasion of privacy. Their attorney argued that "the county disclosed more than what was allowable" under IPRA's exemptions for personnel records.

Sanchez's defense raised the opposite concern: that law enforcement was attempting to silence him for publicizing potential misconduct. "Mr. Sanchez proceeded to post these matters of high public interest and concern to Facebook," his attorney wrote in a motion to dismiss.

A federal judge partially denied the deputies' motion to dismiss in April 2024, allowing Sanchez's underlying wrongful prosecution case to proceed. The litigation continues—years of expensive federal court battles in disputes that reveal a fundamental tension: IPRA mandates broad public access to government records, yet agencies resist disclosure by claiming exemptions. Citizens obtain records and publicize them. Officials sue. Years pass. Taxpayers pay.

The pattern is not accidental. It's designed to make transparency costly and painful.

The Statewide Squeeze: How Officials Are Blocking IPRA and OMA Rights

In Lea County, real-property records disputes led to litigation over IPRA requirements. The New Mexico Court of Appeals ruled the Recording Act governed those particular records, but the case exposed how counties create legal ambiguity to restrict access. Federal litigation continues over similar transparency disputes.

In Alamogordo, the city commission voted 7-0 publicly to hire Dr. Stephanie Hernandez as permanent city manager. Seven weeks later, they reversed that vote— without public explanation nor disclosure of the terms only made available by Alamogordo Town News via IPRA requests. They approved a $485,000+ taxpayer settlement without public debate nor detailed comment. Commissioners held at least 10  executive sessions which are being questioned by citizens and the court filing.

When sued for violating the Open Meetings Act, the city initially moved to squelch a temporary restraining order: More recently they filed a motion. dismiss the case with a hearing scheduled for August 12th. On Friday they rescinded that motion, effectively conceding their legal defense was indefensible as filed and the August 12th dismissal hearing will more than likely be canceled by the court. 

Across all these cases, a consistent strategy emerges: Resist transparency. Use legal technicalities. Delay responses. Withhold records. Characterize transparency requests as "schemes." When forced to court, fight to the last moment, then cave when the legal ground crumbles.

The courts have responded consistently. Judge Ellenwood found Dadzie's restraining order unconstitutional. Federal judges allowed transparency cases to proceed.

The New Mexico Supreme Court issued a landmark May 28, 2026 ruling placing the burden on government agencies to justify record withholding—not on citizens to justify access.

But court victories are costly and slow. Even when citizens win, they've already spent thousands of dollars and months of their lives in time wasted just to seek records that should be easily accessible to the citizens.

This Is About Your Right to Know

Here's what's at stake: Your right to know what your government is doing. Your right to speak about official conduct without fear of litigation. Your right to access public records about how your tax dollars are spent.

When a county director can file a restraining order against a citizen for criticizing his department, what message does that send to the next person thinking about speaking up?

When commissioners can reverse public votes in secret and approve settlements without debate, what control do you have over government decisions?

When agencies can delay IPRA requests indefinitely without penalty, what value does the public records law have?

The pattern across New Mexico shows government officials testing the limits of what they can get away with.

The Rio Arriba case tests whether litigation can silence critics.

The Eddy County case tests whether officials can use counter-suits to intimidate transparency activists. 

The Alamogordo case tests whether technical legal arguments can avoid accountability for secret meetings and hidden reversals.

Each time, courts have sided with citizens. Each time, government loses. But each loss doesn't stop the next official from trying.

What Needs to Change

1. Make Non-Compliance Expensive: If a citizen has to sue to get public records, the government should pay not only attorney fees but for the citizens time and effort. Right now, agencies can delay and obstruct with no real penalty.

2. Protect Transparency Activists: If a government official files a frivolous lawsuit against you for requesting records or criticizing conduct, you should be able to recover your legal fees and have them deferred during the trial process.

The chilling effect works perfectly for the government to silence critics: People see what happened to others and decide it's not worth the risk.

3. Stop Impunity: When officials deliberately obstruct transparency through IPRA delays, improper executive sessions, or litigation against critics, there should be consequences. Discipline. Investigation. Removal from Office. Not just a court ruling that they have to comply next time.

4. Clear Standards: The Attorney General should establish statewide training for government officials on what IPRA requires and what the Open Meetings Act requires. Right now, different agencies use different excuses.

5. Accountability Mechanisms: Establish authority to investigate IPRA and OMA violations and create meaningful disciplinary procedures for officials who obstruct transparency.

The Courts Are Protecting Your Rights—For Now

The New Mexico Supreme Court's May 28, 2026 ruling strengthened protections statewide. Judge Ellenwood's ruling protected Lentini's right to speak. Federal judges allowed transparency cases to proceed when they might have been dismissed on technicalities.

Courts are telling New Mexico government: You cannot suppress speech. You must provide public records. You must hold open meetings.

But here's the reality: Courts can only do so much. They can order records released. They can block unconstitutional restraining orders. They can reject frivolous lawsuits. What they cannot do is make government officials comply voluntarily.

That requires something else. It requires citizens filing IPRA requests and refusing to accept delays. It requires journalists covering government and publicizing obstruction. It requires residents showing up to meetings and demanding answers. It requires people understanding that transparency is not a gift from government—it's a constitutional right.

The Choice Before Us

The Dadzie case. The Eddy County litigation. The Alamogordo meeting violations. These aren't isolated incidents or bureaucratic errors. They're evidence of a statewide pattern—a systematic effort to squeeze the rights that IPRA and the Open Meetings Act provide. Government officials are testing whether they can suppress criticism, block records, and hold secret meetings without consequence.

Across New Mexico, courts have answered: No.

But the tests continue. And they will keep continuing until government agencies understand that resistance is costly and compliance is mandatory.

The question before every New Mexico resident is this: What happens when the courts aren't available? What happens when the next official decides the risk is worth it? What happens if we don't demand that government agencies comply voluntarily with transparency laws?

Your right to know. Your right to question. Your right to hold government accountable. These depend on IPRA working. These depend on the Open Meetings Act being respected. These depend on citizens using these tools and refusing to accept obstruction.

The courts have proven the tools work. Now it's on us to make sure they're used.

Key Court Cases

Ahmed Dadzie v. Cynthia Lentini, Santa Fe District Court (July 24, 2026) - Judge dissolves restraining order as unconstitutional prior restraint on speech

Rostro and Threlkeld v. Eddy County Board of Commissioners and Jason Sanchez, U.S. District Court (January 16, 2024) - Deputies sue over IPRA disclosure; federal judge allows case to proceed

TexasFile LLC v. Board of County Commissioners of Lea County, New Mexico Court of Appeals (February 12, 2019) - Real property records dispute reveals IPRA ambiguity

Tello v. Lea County Board of Commissioners, U.S. District Court (April 2024) - Federal litigation continues over transparency disputes

Edwards v. Alamogordo City Commission, Otero County District Court (June 2026) - City rescinds motion to dismiss Open Meetings Act violations case; heads to trial

New Mexico Supreme Court IPRA Ruling (May 28, 2026) - Landmark decision strengthens public records access standards statewide

item.title: Otero Arts Announces Dynamic Lineup of Exhibitions, Performances, and Creative Workshops for August and September
item.description:
August Exhibitions and Visual Arts

Sue Nichols Retrospective Opens with Reception

The month kicks off with “The Light of La Luz,” a major exhibition of paintings and stained glass by New Mexico artist Sue Nichols. The opening reception is set for August 7 from 5 to 7 p.m. at the Artspace.

The exhibition gathers 33 works in oil, watercolor, and stained glass, representing a career spent studying a single corner of the landscape near La Luz. Nichols, born in Carlsbad and raised in Alamogordo, was working at the Ruidoso Downs racetrack when she met her high school sweetheart and moved to his family’s orchard ranch in the Sacramento Mountains. Her work reflects this deep connection to the region.

The exhibition ranges widely while maintaining a cohesive vision. Paintings exploring working landscapes—including “Way of Life” and “Hell or High Water”—share gallery space with wildlife studies, still life drawings from her home and gardens, and figurative work capturing ordinary people in unguarded moments. The exhibition runs through August 29 and is open to the public Thursdays through Sundays from 1 to 4 p.m

Hands-On Art Workshops

Rock Painting for All Ages

On August 8, Otero Arts offers free rock painting classes for all ages, funded by Thrive! of Southern New Mexico. The workshop runs from 10 a.m. to noon for children ages 6 to 16, and 1 to 3 p.m. for adults 16 and older. Maria Aragon will lead participants in creating colorful painted rocks. Registration is available through www.oteroarts.org or by contacting mariaaragon64@gmail.com.

Photography Printing Workshop with Professional Instruction

On August 17, Ron Kellar, Assistant Professor of Photography at New Mexico State University, will lead a special photography printing workshop sponsored by Center Santa Fe. The workshop runs from 1 to 4 p.m. and will teach participants professional printing techniques using Epson printers. For more information, contact Amber@centersantafe.org.

Film, Lectures, and Community Events

Free Film Screening: “Dean Spanley”

On Friday, August 21, Otero Arts presents a free screening of the English comedy-drama “Dean Spanley” at 5:30 p.m. The film, starring Peter O’Toole and Jeremy North, explores the relationship between a father and son as they reconcile with the help of an extraordinary go-between following the family’s loss of a younger son and mother. The film weaves in themes of loss, healing, and unexpected connections. While free, donations are appreciated.

Archaeological Lecture: Tularosa Canyon Settlement Patterns

On August 18 at 6 p.m., archaeologist Dave Greenwald, President of the Jornada Research Institute (JRI), will present a lecture on settlement and land-use patterns in Tularosa Canyon during the Mesilla Phase (AD 250-1030). Greenwald has been conducting cultural resource management projects in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and west Texas for over 50 years. His 18 years of investigations in the Tularosa area have led to the founding of JRI. The lecture is part of Otero Arts’ partnership with JRI and is free to attend.

September Exhibitions and Performances

Plein Air Painting Exhibition and Reception

September opens with a major group exhibition of landscape paintings. The opening reception is September 4 from 5 to 7 p.m., and the exhibition runs through September 26, open Thursdays through Sundays from 1 to 4 p.m.

“Plein air painting” is a portrait of the landscape in natural light, a genre developed in the 1800s when painters left their dark studios to paint outdoors. Several Otero Arts members have been meeting weekly to paint landscapes in oil, watercolor, pastel, and gouache on location throughout Alamogordo and neighboring towns.

Featured works include “A Welcoming” by Ann Aleshire, “Cottonwood Vista White Sands” by Janet Amtmann, “Abandoned in Bent” by Julie Ford Oliver, and “The Town Pool” by Deirdre Kindthistle. The exhibition remains open to plein air painters in Southern New Mexico. Artists interested in submitting work should visit oteroarts.org for an application. The deadline for submissions is August 20.

Samuel Pollack Concert

On September 18 at 7 p.m., musician Samuel Pollack returns to the Artspace for a concert. Pollack, an Alamogordo native, is a traveling professional musician who has spent over 15 years collecting and mastering rare wind instruments. His repertoire is designed to promote relaxation and healing. Tickets are $15 and can be purchased at oteroarts.org.

“Childhood Remembered” Vocal Recital

Later in September, Otero Arts will host a vocal recital titled “Childhood Remembered” featuring Ann Bagby and Holly Boyle. Details on the specific date are available at oteroarts.org.

September Workshops and Classes

Air Dry Clay Plaque Faces Workshop

On September 12, the second all-ages workshop features air dry clay plaque faces, taught by Maria Aragon. Classes run from 10 a.m. to noon for children ages 6 to 15, and 1 to 3 p.m. for adults 16 and older. Registration is through mariaaragon64@gmail.com or www.oteroarts.org.

Bonus Watercolor Still Life Workshop

On September 13 from 1 to 3 p.m., Janet Amtmann leads a watercolor still life workshop. Participants will learn to choose objects, design the layout, create drawings, and apply watercolor techniques. Contact mariaaragon64@gmail.com to register.

“Desert Reflections & Your Creative Spark” Photography Workshop

On September 26 from 1 to 4 p.m., speaker Leslee Ames-Rogers leads an interactive workshop combining neuroscience with vibrant local artistry. Participants will discover how desert landscapes can unlock creativity and enhance brain health and productivity. The event features free admission with encouraged registration. Call 843-224-5423 to register.

Ongoing Programming

First Thursdays Meet and Greet

On the first Thursday of each month from 10 to 11:30 a.m., Otero Arts hosts informal coffee gatherings featuring community conversation and artist demonstrations. These sessions typically include presentations by featured artists lasting about 20 minutes. Artists and creative makers interested in being featured presenters should contact Ann Beacht at rbeacht@aol.com.

Belly Dance Classes

Ongoing belly dance classes are held every Thursday at 5:30 p.m., led by Claudia Powell. Contact claudia@tularosa.net for details.

Monthly Kids and Adults Free Workshops

Free workshops are held the second Saturday of each month for all ages.

The Artspace Rental and Ongoing Events

The historic, beautifully restored Otero Artspace at Indiana Avenue and 12th Street is available for rent for private and public events. Currently, the space hosts several regular community programs, including a writers group (Monday nights), poetry group meetings (twice monthly), and belly dance classes (Thursday evenings). For rental rates and availability, call 575-446-3880 or visit oteroarts.org.

How to Get Involved

Otero Arts invites community members to participate in these programs, volunteer as workshop leaders, or help support the organization’s mission. All events are designed to be accessible, welcoming, and enriching for people of all ages and abilities. For more information about any event, visit www.oteroarts.org or contact the Artspace at 575-446-3880.

item.title: Alamogordo Town News Theatrical Review: A Glorious Burst of Joy: Sister Act Celebrates Alamogordo’s Talent and Spirit
item.description:
★★★★★ HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

There are nights when you leave the theater with your heart soaring and a smile you can’t wipe off your face.

The Alamogordo Music Theater’s production of Sister Act at the Flickinger Center is exactly that kind of evening—a celebration of our community’s extraordinary talent, infectious joy, and the transformative power of theater created by neighbors for neighbors.

This Tony-nominated musical comedy, based on the beloved 1992 film, could easily have been a simple retelling. Instead, under the spirited direction of Jeanette Borunda, it becomes something genuinely magical: a high-energy, feel-good experience that reminds you why you love live theater—and why you should support it passionately.

Our Stars Shine Bright

Rosie Daffern’s performance as Deloris Van Cartier is revelatory. This Alamogordo talent commands the stage with star quality, bringing the perfect blend of sass, vulnerability, and showstopping vocals. When this disco diva first arrives at the convent, the contrast is hilarious, but Daffern mines genuine character development from Deloris’s journey—her transformation feels earned, not forced. Her voice is powerful and precise, perfectly suited to Alan Menken’s dynamic score. This is the kind of performance that makes you proud to call her a neighbor.

Sarah Harshey’s portrayal of the formidable Mother Superior is equally stellar. Harshey brings warmth, nuance, and subtle humor to a character that could easily fall flat, creating a Mother Superior who is both stern and deeply human. The chemistry between Daffern and Harshey is one of the production’s true delights—you genuinely believe in their contentious but ultimately loving relationship.

The supporting cast is equally impressive. Loren Jackson brings gravitas and charm to Monsignor O’Hara, while Pary Bennett and Nick Harshey create a believable criminal underworld subplot with surprising depth and comedic timing. These local performers elevate every scene they’re in, proving that Alamogordo has world-class talent right here in our own backyard.

A Convent Full of Heart and Alamogordo Soul

The ensemble of convent sisters shines brilliantly. Bella Ochoa as Sister Mary Robert, Amy Bethard as Sister Mary Patrick, Robin Milne as Sister Mary Lazarus, Renee Hirte as Sister Mary Theresa, and Mary Lynn Bardocz as Sister Mary Martin-of-Tours create a genuine sisterhood that’s both touching and thoroughly entertaining. Watch how these performers interact: this is clearly a cast that has bonded, rehearsed together, and genuinely cares about telling this story. That authentic connection translates beautifully to the audience.

But the heart of this production extends far beyond the convent walls. The supporting cast members—Tyler Wren Hutchens as TJ, Gabe Mauger as Joey, Chris Medina as Pablo, Ardrianna Sharp as Michelle, Cory Nielsen as Tina, and Elijah Strickland as Ernie—each bring specificity and life to their roles. These are our community members, many of whom work day jobs, volunteer for causes, and live on our streets. Seeing them transform into fully realized characters on stage is a gift.

The Ensemble: Alamogordo’s Heart on Display

And then there’s the ensemble—the true backbone of this production: Clifford Cabos, Chance Cass, Patrick Cruz, Hannah DeLay, Isabelle Furman, Katie Grabowski, Anthony Hayman, Kierstin Johnson, Amelia Lehmuth, Trinity Lipsey, Aiden Mai, Crystal Morris, Beck Natalini, Jeremy Patton, Kitanna Pichay, Kayla Sandoval, Zachary Stewart, Jonece Tallant, Rebecca Ward, Priscilla Weber, and Dakota Zapata.

These thirty-plus performers create the texture and energy that makes this production feel truly alive. The ensemble work is tight, the choreography is crisp, and the harmonies showcase the breadth of vocal talent in Alamogordo’s theater community. When you watch this group move across the stage together, you’re witnessing the true spirit of our town—people who come together, support each other, and create something beautiful.

The Music and the Message

Alan Menken’s score is as charming and accessible here as ever, and the live orchestration brings richness to every number. From the opening “Raise Your Voice” to the joyful chaos of the final act, the music propels the story forward with infectious energy. The standout “Sister Act” number is a showstopper that will have you grinning from ear to ear and likely humming for days afterward.

Why This Matters: Community Theater as a Community Treasure

In an age of streaming services and passive entertainment, there’s something profoundly important about gathering together to watch live performance created by people we know and love. The Alamogordo Music Theater, now in its 54th year of operation, represents something irreplaceable: a space where artists can flourish, where creativity thrives, and where community bonds strengthen.

This production is a testament to what happens when talented people invest their time, energy, and passion into something greater than themselves. Behind every performance on that stage are countless hours of rehearsal, countless moments of vulnerability, and countless acts of commitment. These are neighbors supporting neighbors. This is culture, created locally, for our community.

The Flickinger Center provides the perfect setting for this production—an elegant venue that elevates the theatrical experience while remaining accessible and welcoming to all. When you support local theater like Sister Act, you’re not just buying a ticket; you’re investing in the cultural vitality of Alamogordo, supporting the arts education initiatives that the Alamogordo Music Theater has championed for over five decades, and providing opportunities for young people to discover the transformative power of performance.

Entertainment for Everyone—A Gift for Our Community

What makes this production special is how it works on multiple levels. If you loved the original film, you’ll appreciate the cleverness of the adaptation and how the story expands with music. If you’ve never seen it, you’ll find yourself swept up in a story about acceptance, redemption, and the unexpected ways people can inspire each other. There’s humor for adults, heart for everyone, and pure fun throughout.

This is also a show that the whole family can enjoy together—grandparents, parents, teenagers, and children all leave the theater smiling. In our complex world, that’s a rare and beautiful gift.

A Testament to Who We Are

Sister Act showcases what Alamogordo is truly capable of. We have talent here. We have dedication here. We have people who care about excellence and community. This production proves it night after night. When you watch Rosie Daffern transform the stage, when you hear the convent choir soar through a Menken melody, when you see the entire cast come together in that joyful finale—you’re witnessing what happens when a community believes in itself and its artists.

Final Verdict

Sister Act is exactly what you need right now: an evening of laughter, stunning performances by your neighbors, beautiful music, and the reminder that magic happens when a talented community comes together to create something joyful. Leave your house. Come to the Flickinger Center. Support the people who live on your street and share your community. You will leave smiling, uplifted, and grateful to live in a place with this kind of artistic heart.

Why You Should Go: Because live theater created by your neighbors lifts the spirit in ways that screens cannot. Because community talent deserves celebration and support. Because you’ll leave smiling and humming “Raise Your Voice” for days. Because Alamogordo has something special to be proud of. Because this is your community’s theater. Because every single person on that stage is your neighbor, your friend, your community—and they deserve your support.

Sister Act runs through August 8, 2026, at the Flickinger Center for Performing Arts. Performances are at 7:00 PM (Friday and Saturday) and 2:00 PM (Sunday Matinee). Tickets are $15.48.

For more information and to purchase tickets, visit www.alamogordomusictheatre.org or call (575) 437-2202.

Support local. Support the arts. Support your community’s artists. You won’t regret it.

item.title: A Night in the Museum: Alamogordo’s Living History Came Alive in Ambitious Community Celebration
item.description:
Alamogordo NM- The Tularosa Basin Historical Society delivered an evening of pure magic this past weekend with “A Night in the Museum”—an innovative and ambitiously creative event that reminded everyone why preserving and celebrating our region’s history matters so deeply.

This remarkable achievement belongs first and foremost to the visionary leadership of Debra and Joe Lewandowski, whose stewardship of the Tularosa Basin Museum of History has transformed it into the cultural heart of our community. Under their dedicated direction, the museum has become far more than a repository of artifacts—it is a living, breathing center for historical engagement and community connection. The Lewandowskis’ commitment to bringing history to life was on full display this weekend, as they orchestrated an ambitious event that required meticulous planning, creative vision, and unwavering dedication.

What could have been a traditional museum experience transformed into something far more powerful: a living, breathing celebration of the Tularosa Basin’s remarkable heritage. From the moment guests arrived, they were transported through time by passionate historical interpreters who brought authentic characters to life with meticulous attention to detail and genuine enthusiasm for sharing their stories.

Leadership That Inspires Excellence

The success of “A Night in the Museum” stands as a testament to the Lewandowskis’ leadership. Rather than simply managing a museum, they have cultivated a culture of engaged stewardship—one where volunteers feel inspired to go above and beyond, where creative possibilities are explored and celebrated, and where every community member is invited to participate in preserving and sharing our heritage.

Working alongside a dedicated staff of volunteers, the Lewandowskis transformed the museum into an interactive stage where history became palpable. Their ability to recruit, inspire, and coordinate volunteers speaks to the respect they have earned and the trust the community places in their vision. These aren’t passive exhibits maintained by a small professional staff—they are vibrant installations brought to life by passionate community members who understand that this work matters.

The Lewandowskis’ continued success as the linchpin of leadership for the Tularosa Basin Historical Society ensures that initiatives like this evening will continue to thrive. Their willingness to take creative risks, embrace ambitious projects such as the Dudley School project, and empower volunteers has established a sustainable model for cultural preservation that strengthens with each event.
