The evening’s commanding presence came from City Commissioner Warren Robinson, whose portrayal of a Buffalo Soldier transcended simple costuming. In full period military regalia with dignified bearing, Commissioner Robinson embodied the courage, sacrifice, and pride of the African American soldiers whose contributions fundamentally shaped the American West. His authentic engagement with visitors—sharing stories, explaining the significance of the uniform, and connecting the Buffalo Soldier legacy to our region’s own history—transformed this into a deeply moving tribute to often-overlooked heroes. Commissioner Robinson’s willingness to step into this role sent a powerful message: our elected officials understand that honoring all chapters of our history is essential work.

The ranger from White Sands National Park engaged families with captivating storytelling about one of the region’s most iconic landmarks, creating magical moments as children’s eyes lit up learning about the park’s unique landscape and history. Local doctor Rick Miller brought remarkable depth to his portrayal as a skilled potter and artisan, sitting authentically among display cases and sharing the craftsmanship traditions of La Luz Pottery.

A railroad conductor character in period dress engaged visitors with tales of the locomotives that once connected this remote region to the wider world.

Filmmaker Larry Sheffield: Preserving Our Stories for Tomorrow

Perhaps most instrumental to the evening’s broader mission was the presence and passion of award-winning filmmaker Larry Sheffield. Sheffield’s dedication to documenting and preserving the Tularosa Basin’s rich history extends far beyond a single evening—it represents a lifelong commitment to ensuring that the stories of this region don’t fade with time.

Sheffield’s work as a filmmaker has already become invaluable to the community. His projects capture not just events and landscapes, but the human dimensions of our history—the voices, the emotions, the lived experiences that statistics and photographs alone cannot convey. By attending “A Night in the Museum,” Sheffield demonstrated his ongoing investment in this mission while also elevating the event itself. His presence signaled to the community that this work matters, that it’s worthy of serious artistic attention, and that the stories being shared deserve to be preserved in multiple formats for future generations.

Sheffield’s role exemplifies what it means to be a cultural steward. He doesn’t simply document history as an observer; he actively participates in creating spaces where history comes alive. His passion for the region’s heritage is contagious, inspiring others—from museum volunteers to city officials to visitors—to see their own community’s past with new appreciation and urgency. In a time when so many local stories risk being lost, Sheffield’s commitment to filmmaking ensures that the Tularosa Basin’s narrative will endure, reaching audiences far beyond our region and teaching others about who we are and where we come from.

Mayor McDonald and the Miami Street Legacy

Mayor Sharon McDonald brought crucial perspective and leadership to the Miami Street experience exhibit—one of the evening’s most vital presentations. The Miami Street story was pieced together by Mayor McDonald and Sherri Vesta Edmonds and represents a pivotal and often-overlooked chapter of Alamogordo’s identity. Mayor McDonald and Ms. Edmonds involvement in helping craft and guide this narrative demonstrates municipal and community leadership commitment to telling the complete history of our community.

Working alongside community historians and former residents, Mayor McDonald who was assisted by Sherri Vesta Edmonds and others helped ensure that the Miami Street experience was presented with authenticity, respect, and the prominence it deserves. Her participation underscored that this history—the thriving African American community district, the cultural richness, the resilience of its people—is not peripheral to Alamogordo’s story. It is central to who we are. By actively engaging visitors and sharing the significance of Miami Street’s legacy, Mayor McDonald made clear that current city leadership understands the importance of honoring all chapters of our community’s past and ensuring future generations know the complete truth of where they come from.

Voices That Bridge Past and Present

The “Black History in the Tularosa Basin” and “Miami Street Legacy” exhibits stood as powerful centerpieces, showcasing the contributions, resilience, and joy of African American communities in our region. Former Dudley School alumni sharing personal memories transformed dusty history into lived experience—stories of classrooms, friendships, and formative years that shaped who they became. This intergenerational dialogue proved that history isn’t something confined to textbooks or museum labels; it lives and breathes in the people of our community.

Why This Matters for Alamogordo

Events like “A Night in the Museum” serve a crucial purpose in our community. In an era when history can feel distant and abstract, this evening proved that heritage is personal, accessible, and worth celebrating together. The enthusiastic turnout—families with children, longtime residents, visitors discovering our region for the first time—demonstrated something vital: Alamogordo residents deeply value understanding where we come from and who we are.

The museum itself transforms into more than a building—it becomes a sanctuary for these stories, a gathering place where past and present meet, where children see their community’s full legacy as something worthy of pride and study, and where every visitor leaves with a deeper, more complete understanding of this remarkable region.

A Thank You to Our Community’s Heart

Special recognition goes to CHRISTUS Health, the Tularosa Basin Historical Society, the Toy Train Depot, NMSBVI, La Luz Pottery, Our Country Kitchen, and all generous sponsors, donors, volunteers, and historical interpreters. The care evident in every detail—from meticulously researched costumes to thoughtfully curated exhibits to meaningful keepsakes sent home with guests—reflects a community that honors its heritage in its entirety.

Most importantly, our deepest gratitude goes to Debra and Joe Lewandowski for their visionary leadership of the Tularosa Basin Museum of History. Their dedication, creative direction, and ability to inspire a team of passionate volunteers made this ambitious event possible. Under their stewardship, the museum has become an indispensable institution—the linchpin holding together our community’s commitment to historical preservation and cultural celebration. They have shown us that with creativity, passion, and community collaboration, history isn’t something we observe from a distance; it becomes something we live and celebrate together.

Every volunteer who stepped into character demonstrated what passionate community engagement looks like. City Commissioner Warren Robinson’s powerful portrayal of the Buffalo Soldier, filmmaker Larry Sheffield’s visible commitment to preserving our stories, and Mayor McDonald’s stewardship of the Miami Street narrative each showed what true cultural leadership means—active participation in honoring and perpetuating the complete narratives that define us.

A Night to Remember

Here in Alamogordo, history isn’t confined to dusty archives—it’s woven into our landscapes, preserved in our community, and close enough to touch. A Night in the Museum proved we have the creativity, passion, and community spirit to celebrate it in extraordinary ways. More importantly, it demonstrated our commitment to telling complete stories with authenticity and reverence—including the vital, living legacy of Miami Street and all the African American communities whose resilience and contributions shaped the Tularosa Basin.

It’s a powerful reminder of why Alamogordo is a great place to live, visit, and belong. And it’s a testament to the power of visionary community leaders like Debra and Joe Lewandowski who refuse to let our stories fade away.

We can’t wait for next year, but don’t wait until next year visit the museum anytime of the year and learn the rich history.

item.title: In Memory of Charlie Mendez
item.description:
Charlie Mendez was a man of remarkable faith, strength, kindness, and generosity. A cattleman at heart, Charlie believed in hard work and took great pride in sharing what he knew with others. He was always willing to teach anyone who wanted to learn, but one of the things he loved sharing most was the Word of God. His faith was a guiding force throughout his life, and he was always willing to speak about the Lord with anyone willing to listen.

Charlie loved music and worship. He found great joy in playing his guitar, singing, and being a part of the church choir. His faith wasn't something he simply spoke about-it could be seen in the way he lived and in the way he treated others.

He had an extraordinarily giving heart. Charlie was always willing to lend a helping hand to someone in need. If he saw someone standing on a street corner asking for money, he would give what he had, even if it was his last cent. If someone needed a ride, he would take them. If someone needed help, he found a way to help. He never needed recognition or anything in return. Giving to others was simply part of who Charlie was.

Charlie was also an incredibly strong man with a positive outlook on life. It seemed that very little could overwhelm or stress him. When those around him were worried, Charlie had a way of remaining steady. He could be the calm in any storm, offering strength and reassurance simply through his presence.

That strength stayed with Charlie throughout his final journey. He had an incredible will to live and fought with everything he had to remain with the people he loved for as long as he possibly could. His determination and courage were a reflection of the way he lived his entire life-with faith, hope, strength, and perseverance.

Charlie shared his life with his beloved wife, Olivia Mendez, and was a loving father to April Mendez, Jose Mendez, Ernie Mendez, Angelica Frias, Dominic Mendez, Sonya Morin, Rebeca Mendez, and Warren Mendez. He was also a proud and loving Grandpa, Great-Grandpa and Great uncle to all of his grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and nieces and nephews cherishing each of them deeply and holding a special place in his heart for every one of them. His family was blessed to know the strength of his love, the comfort of his presence, and the example he set throughout his life.

Charlie's legacy cannot be measured simply by the years he lived. It lives in the lessons he taught, the people he helped, the songs he sang, the music he played, the faith he shared, and the family he loved so deeply.

Although saying goodbye leaves an emptiness that words cannot fully express, there is comfort in knowing how deeply Charlie loved God. The faith he spent his life sharing with others now gives us hope that he has been called home to the Lord he loved and served so faithfully.

His life was a blessing.

His strength was an example.

His generosity was a gift.

His faith was an inspiration.

And being loved by him was one of the greatest gifts our family could have ever received.

Charlie will forever be our husband, our dad, our grandpa, our great-grandpa, our teacher, our brother, our friend, and our calm in every storm. His love and the lessons he left behind will remain in our hearts for generations to come.

item.title: CRISIS: Tularosa Declares Emergency Water Shortage — Complete Watering Ban Enacted
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Village of Tularosa has declared a critical water emergency and issued an immediate, total ban on all outdoor watering. Water storage tanks are nearly empty, prompting village officials to take unprecedented enforcement action.

“We are in a crisis with our water situation and our tanks are almost empty at this point,” village officials stated in an emergency community alert. “We really need everyone to abide by the NO WATERING restriction and minimize water usage for daily use.”

The emergency arrives amid a statewide crisis. Approximately 94% of New Mexico is under drought conditions as of July 21, 2026, placing the 2,593-resident Otero County community on the front lines of the state’s water emergency.

Zero-Tolerance Enforcement

Tularosa is not requesting voluntary compliance—officials have made clear that enforcement will be swift. According to official notices, “Anyone observed watering during these restrictions will be issued a citation.” The Tularosa Police Department is actively monitoring compliance, with violators facing legal consequences and fines.

Effective immediately, all outdoor watering is prohibited—including landscape watering of lawns and gardens, lawn maintenance, and decorative water features such as fountains. Village officials emphasize this is not an inconvenience but a mandatory emergency measure to protect critical water supplies.

Community Response Needed — Daily Use Must Be Reduced

The watering ban extends to all outdoor use, but village officials are also calling residents to reduce daily household water consumption. Water plant operators are working overtime to manage the emergency. “Our water plant operators are working around the clock and doing everything they can to keep water flowing and replenish our storage,” village leadership stated.

Despite the clear warning, officials have heard from residents claiming they plan to violate the restrictions. “Comments from people saying they’re going to water anyway or that the restrictions don’t matter are concerning,” officials noted. “The reality is that they do matter. Every gallon that is conserved today helps protect our community’s water supply for tomorrow.”

Village leaders are clear about priorities: preserving water for household consumption, drinking water, sanitation, emergency services, fire protection, and critical infrastructure like hospitals and schools.

“Tularosa has always been a community that steps up when it matters most. This is one of those times,” village leadership appealed to residents.

Steps Residents Must Take

Officials urge immediate household-level action: shorter showers, full laundry loads, and efficient dishwashing. Fix leaking faucets immediately—even small drips add up during a crisis. Suspend car washing and do not fill or top off swimming pools or decorative fountains. On outdoor landscaping, consider temporary reliance on drought-resistant plants.

The situation is indefinite. “It is unknown when the restriction will be lifted,” officials stated, making this a long-term commitment for the community, not a temporary inconvenience.

Part of Statewide Water Emergency

Tularosa’s crisis is not isolated. Scientists predict New Mexico will face a shortage of 750,000 acre-feet of water within 50 years as climate change causes temperatures to rise — reducing snowpack and runoff. More immediately, when today’s high school graduates reach retirement age, New Mexico will have 25% less water than it currently has in already over-stressed communities and farms.

The Tularosa Basin’s geography compounds the problem. Ground water is recharged primarily from precipitation falling on Sierra Blanca, with as little as 7.5% of this precipitation estimated to reach the aquifers in the mountain areas. With limited recharge rates and sustained drought conditions, the region’s water vulnerability is severe.

Long-Term Solution: Brackish Water Desalination Project

Village officials are not waiting for state-level solutions. Tularosa is pursuing a long-planned brackish water treatment project. The project draws on the village’s Montezuma Well groundwater rights and would treat brackish groundwater—with total dissolved solids around 2,500 milligrams per liter—through a reverse osmosis system housed in a roughly 60-by-100-foot building near the village’s existing water tank site, recovering about 82 percent of pumped water as usable supply.

The timeline is critical: Construction is estimated to begin around spring 2027 and take approximately 15 months. This means the emergency restrictions will remain in place through at least late 2027, possibly into 2028.

Tularosa’s approach aligns with state strategy. New Mexico is systematically exploring deep brackish groundwater as a supplemental water supply, which can be treated through reverse osmosis for potable water and irrigation. The region benefits from existing research infrastructure—the Tularosa Basin National Desalination Research Facility was established in Alamogordo in 2004 as a joint project of the Federal Bureau of Reclamation and Sandia National Laboratories.

The village is also reaching out for external assistance. “We are currently reaching out for help for this situation,” officials stated, indicating that state and federal resources will be needed to supplement local efforts.

What’s at Stake

For Tularosa residents accustomed to a small-town rhythm, this crisis represents an unprecedented test. The village has no flexibility—compliance is not optional. The desalination project offers hope for 2028, but until then, Tularosa faces months of restricted water and enforced conservation. Village leaders are counting on residents to understand the stakes: fire protection, emergency services, drinking water, and the village’s long-term survival.

The region’s broader context—a state losing a quarter of its water over the next 25 years—underscores that Tularosa’s crisis is not unique. Other New Mexico communities will likely face similar emergencies if conservation efforts fail and long-term water infrastructure projects lag. For now, all eyes are on Tularosa, where a community of 2,593 people faces the harsh reality that water—long taken for granted in residential life—is the rarest resource of all.

item.title: Free Community Event Features “First We Bombed New Mexico” Documentary and Panel Discussion
item.description:
Alamogordo NM- Alamogordo residents are invited to a free screening of the powerful documentary “First We Bombed New Mexico” this Thursday, August 12, at the Flickinger Center for Performing Arts.

The documentary explores the profound impact of the Trinity Site atomic bomb test on Otero County and the surrounding region, examining the historical events and long-term consequences of the 1945 test at White Sands Missile Range.

Event Details

Date: Thursday, August 12, 2026

Time: Doors open at 5:30 PM | Film begins at 6:00 PM

Location: Flickinger Theater

1110 N New York Ave, Alamogordo, NM 88310

Cost: Free admission – All welcome

Discussion with Local Leaders

Following the screening, attendees will have the opportunity to participate in a live discussion with:

• Lois Lipman – Director and Producer

• Rep. Gabe Vasquez – U.S. Representative (NM-02)

• Deb Haaland – Democratic Candidate for Governor

This panel discussion will allow community members to engage directly with local and state leaders about the film’s themes and the Trinity Site’s ongoing significance to Otero County and New Mexico.

About the Documentary

First We Bombed New Mexico, directed and produced by Lois Lipman, originally premiered in 2023 and was revised following pivotal legislative changes in 2025. The documentary examines the long-term impacts of the July 16, 1945 Trinity nuclear test—the world’s first atomic bomb detonation—on nearby New Mexico communities, with particular focus on a group known as the “Downwinders.”

The film centers on the largely untold story of the Downwinders: primarily Hispanic and Native American residents of the Tularosa Basin and surrounding areas who were exposed to radioactive fallout without warning or evacuation. Through personal narratives and decades of advocacy, the documentary follows Tina Cordova, a cancer survivor and co-founder of the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium, as she leads a multigenerational fight for recognition and compensation.

First We Bombed New Mexico shines light on the government secrecy and negligence that left countless families vulnerable to radiation exposure, and traces the multigenerational health effects—particularly cancer—that have plagued Downwinder communities for over 75 years. A significant chapter of the film’s narrative involves the eventual expansion of the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) in July 2025, which for the first time included New Mexico Downwinders in federal compensation programs.

The film has screened widely at festivals and community events throughout New Mexico and beyond, often accompanied by Q&A sessions with director Lipman and Cordova. This Alamogordo screening provides a rare opportunity to engage directly with these voices of resilience and advocacy.

About the Event

This screening is organized as part of the 2026 gubernatorial campaign, with support from Deb Haaland for New Mexico. The event brings together key voices in New Mexico’s nuclear justice movement and political leadership.

Director and Producer Lois Lipman will be present to discuss the film and her years of work documenting the Downwinders’ stories and advocacy efforts. Audiences will have the opportunity to engage with her insights into how the film came together and its impact on public awareness.

U.S. Representative Gabe Vasquez (NM-02) represents the congressional district that includes Otero County and surrounding communities. Vasquez has been actively engaged with the issues of environmental justice and addressing the long-term health and economic impacts of nuclear testing on New Mexico communities.

Deb Haaland, the Democratic nominee for Governor (having won the primary in June 2026), brings a long track record of advocating for environmental justice, indigenous rights, and accountability for historical wrongs. These issues are intrinsically tied to New Mexico’s nuclear history and the experiences of the Downwinders, many of whom are Native American and Hispanic communities.

Why This Matters for Otero County

This screening and discussion provides residents an opportunity to engage with their community’s complex story told with nuance and respect. The Trinity Site’s legacy continues to shape conversations about environmental policy, public health, and New Mexico’s role in American history. The panel format allows for direct dialogue with regional and state leaders about how we remember, learn from, and move forward with this critical chapter of our past.

item.title: Otero and Rupp Present Facts Transparently: Tularosa Faces Critical Water Crisis; Village Moves to Address Emergency
item.description:
Tularosa, NM — The Village of Tularosa is confronting a critical water shortage that has forced officials to declare a formal emergency and implement a mandatory outdoor watering ban. In an emergency meeting Monday, the Village Council will vote on Resolution #2026-2027-9 while village leadership has outline both immediate relief measures and longer-term infrastructure solutions via social media communications. 

Water storage tanks have reached dangerously low levels. Commissioner Christopher Rupp explained why conservation is critical: “This is not simply about watering lawns or gardens. This is about ensuring that every home has water available for drinking, cooking, sanitation, and that adequate water is available for emergency services.”

Immediate and Long-Term Response

Trustee Casey Otero announced that the village has begun receiving emergency assistance from Oasis Enterprises to bring in additional water supplies. She emphasized the village’s comprehensive approach: “We are also actively exploring every other available option. These types of issues cannot be fixed overnight, but please know that we are working diligently to find both immediate and long-term solutions.”

The infrastructure challenges facing Tularosa are longstanding. Rupp noted: “These issues have existed for many years, well before the current Mayor and Board of Trustees took office. While the current administration inherited these longstanding infrastructure challenges, the Board has been actively working to address them.”

Since taking office, the Board has pursued:

• Securing additional water resources

• Repairing and improving existing infrastructure

• Seeking funding opportunities for long-term improvements

“Although projects of this size take time due to engineering, permitting, and funding requirements, the Board has recently made significant progress toward addressing these critical needs,” Rupp said.

Important Updates and Clarifications

Otero addressed several critical points: The village is awaiting legal guidance on certain aspects of the response. “We are still waiting on guidance from our attorney regarding certain parts of this situation, so I don’t have all of the answers just yet. As soon as we receive that information, we will share it with the community,” he said.

Regarding concerns about the upcoming school year: “This situation will not impact the start of the school year. Students will have access to drinking water and restrooms, so there is no concern in that regard.”

What Residents Must Do

The Village is asking residents to immediately implement the following conservation practices:

Outdoor:

• Complete ban on outdoor watering for lawns, gardens, and landscaping

Indoor:

• Take shorter showers

• Run laundry and dishwashers only with full loads

• Repair water leaks promptly

• Report significant water leaks to the Village immediately

Otero emphasized the personal stakes: “I received my own utility bill yesterday, and you’ll notice there is also a message asking residents to restrict outdoor watering. Every gallon we can conserve right now makes a difference.”

Community Response and Recognition

Village officials acknowledged public frustration while calling for unity. Otero stated: “I know everyone is frustrated, and I completely understand those feelings. Thank you to everyone who is conserving water, being patient, and supporting one another during this challenging time.”

Rupp reinforced the message of collective action: “Tularosa has always been a community that comes together when faced with challenges. By conserving water now and continuing to support investments in our infrastructure, we can help ensure a stronger and more reliable water system for generations to come.”

Rupp also expressed gratitude to village staff: “I want to express my appreciation to our water plant operators, Public Works employees, emergency responders, and everyone working behind the scenes to address this situation. Their dedication and hard work during this difficult time are greatly appreciated.”

Next Steps

The next regular council meeting is scheduled for August 19, 2026. For accessibility accommodations, questions about the emergency measures, or to report water leaks, residents can contact the Village Clerk at 585-2771.

item.title: Village Board Passes Resolution Amid Critical Tank Levels Caused by Wildfire Debris - Mayor Cooksey
item.description:
Alamogordo, NM — The Village of Tularosa has declared a formal water emergency and enacted an immediate ban on all outdoor watering, following a dramatic drop in municipal water storage levels. The emergency resolution (NO. 2026-2027-9) was passed and adopted by the Village Board on August 3rd, 2026, as water tank levels plummeted from 16 feet to just 6 feet overnight.

The crisis stems from recent heavy monsoon rains in the upper watershed and neighboring Ruidoso area that washed wildfire ash, soot, and debris into the Tularosa regional water sources. According to Mayor Debbie Cooksey, the contaminated water cannot be processed through standard treatment facilities without risking damage to filters and pumps that could cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to replace.

“We can’t process water like that,” Mayor Cooksey explained during an interview conducted Sunday. “It’s mud, not water. We have to let it settle down before we can bring it into our holding pond.”

Emergency Response Underway

To address the immediate crisis, the Village has deployed several emergency measures:

• A potable water truck is delivering approximately 6,000 gallons of treated water daily directly into the fresh water system

• Multiple loads have already been delivered, with plans for continued deliveries

• Community members and local farmers have offered additional water support

• Water-intensive businesses, including restaurants with commercial dishwashers, were asked to voluntarily close operations

“We’ve had a tremendous turnout of people offering to help us,” Mayor Cooksey said, noting that all but two restaurants complied with closure requests.

Mandatory Restrictions in Effect

Section 2 of the resolution explicitly prohibits:

• Lawn sprinking

• Watering of gardens and landscaping

• Washing of vehicles or driveways

• Filling or topping off swimming pools, hot tubs, and decorative fountains

All residents and commercial enterprises are urged to practice severe indoor water conservation, including shorter showers, running only full loads of laundry and dishes, and repairing active plumbing leaks.

The restrictions remain in force for an initial seven-day period, or until further notice is provided by Village administration upon verification that water treatment capabilities and tank levels have safely recovered.

Enforcement and Penalties

The Tularosa Police Department and municipal code enforcement officers are authorized to issue immediate citations and fines to anyone observed violating the outdoor watering prohibition. Violations can result in penalties up to $500 or 90 days in jail, according to municipal ordinance.

“We ran around and made sure nobody was watering,” Mayor Cooksey said of the enforcement efforts over the weekend. “If we didn’t stop this, we would not have had enough water. We would have woke up this morning with no water.”

Timeline for Recovery

The mayor estimates that restrictions may need to remain in place for approximately three weeks, coinciding with the end of monsoon season—currently halfway through its cycle.

“Once the monsoon season ends, we should be fine,” Mayor Cooksey stated. “But monsoon season is not over, and every time it rains up there, it’s gonna affect us down here.”

Mayor’s Message to Residents

Mayor Cooksey issued a direct appeal to Tularosa residents to comply with the restrictions:

“Please do not water. If you care about Tularosa at all, and you love living here, abide by our rule and not water. I’ve got 7 rose bushes and 8 or 9 plants in my yard, but if they die, they die. It’s only plants and grass. If we don’t have any water to shower, or to flush our toilets, or to drink, that’s a real big issue.”

For more information or questions regarding the water emergency and restrictions, residents can contact Mayor Cooksey, the Village trustees, or the Tularosa Village office. Contact numbers are available on the Village of Tularosa website.

Wendy Urquuidez, Runner’s Refuge — Urquuidez a volunteer in the operations for Runner’s Refuge, a food and resource center that serves approximately 175 people several days a week through donations alone. At a recent City Commission meeting, Urquuidez highlighted multi-county collaboration on homelessness funding and shared real-world examples of acute community need. “We see firsthand the gaps in services,” Urquuidez explained, underscoring the urgency of projects like the Dream Center.

Nadia Sikes, 100% Otero Housing Action Team — Sikes leads housing advocacy work for 100% Otero, a grassroots nonprofit dedicated to eliminating childhood trauma while ensuring all county residents have access to ten vital services for surviving and thriving, with housing as a cornerstone. As a commissioner on the Eastern Regional Housing Authority (ERHA) Board, Sikes has documented homeless encampments throughout the county and advocated for systemic change. “The homelessness crisis in Alamogordo and communities across the state and country must be addressed,” Sikes has emphasized. “We have to support organizations working to make housing accessible to all.”

Alamo City Dream Center Representative — A spokesperson from Mountain View Church’s Dream Center initiative will present details on the facility’s mission and services.

The Alamo City Dream Center: A New Resource for Alamogordo

The Alamo City Dream Center represents a major expansion of community support for people experiencing homelessness. Originally conceived by Pastor Anthony Torres and his wife Sasha Torres of Mountain View Church, the Dream Center builds on a decade of emergency shelter operations, free funeral services, and disaster relief that has served hundreds of families.

The proposed facility will provide:

• Emergency shelter with showers and laundry facilities

• Hot meals and a soup kitchen serving free community meals Monday–Friday starting at 4:00 p.m.

• Storm shelter and emergency disaster relief capacity

• Stable, permanent infrastructure designed to serve Otero County residents indefinitely

In June 2026, the Alamogordo City Commission unanimously voted to allocate $200,000 in state opioid settlement funds to support the project’s development. The facility is estimated to cost approximately $1.9 million for core construction.

Addressing a Growing Crisis

The urgency of these efforts cannot be overstated. A January 2023 Point-in-Time Count documented 49 unsheltered individuals in Otero County, though advocates note the actual figure is likely higher, as this vulnerable population is difficult to count. The visible increase in homelessness downtown has prompted city leaders to balance compassionate support with public safety concerns.

Why This Forum Matters

Residents will have the opportunity to ask questions and engage directly with practitioners working daily to address homelessness. The forum offers a rare chance to hear from:

• Direct service providers managing food distribution and emergency shelter

• Housing advocates tracking data and advocating for systemic solutions

• Faith-based leadership implementing permanent infrastructure

“These are not abstract discussions,” said one community observer. “Wendy and Nadia and the Dream Center team are doing the actual work. This forum gives people a chance to understand what’s happening and how they can support these efforts.”

Event Details

What: Voices of Alamogordo Community Forum – Alamo City Dream Center and Unhoused Discussion 

Otero Arts 1118 Indiana, Tuesday, August 4, 2026 at 6:00 PM hosted by 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News 

Cost: Free

Format Style: Salon-style community dialog with Q&A

For more information, visit 2ndlifemediaalamogordo.town.news or follow @AlamogordoN on social media.

Supporting the Unhoused Community

Residents interested in supporting these efforts can:

• Donate to Runner’s Refuge (accepts monetary and in-kind donations)

• Volunteer with 100% Otero’s housing and community initiatives

• Contact Mountain View Church about donations or volunteering for the Dream Center

• Attend city commission meetings to advocate for housing-focused policy

“Community change happens when residents show up, ask questions, and support the organizations doing this work,” host Edwards notes. “This forum is an opportunity to learn, connect, and be part of the solution.”

item.title: City withdraws motion to dismiss Open Meetings Act lawsuit over city manager hiring, will answer by Aug. 14
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Alamogordo City Commission has withdrawn its motion to dismiss a lawsuit accusing it of violating the state's Open Meetings Act during the process that led to the hiring of City Manager Robert Stockwell, according to a notice filed in the Twelfth Judicial District Court.

The notice, filed July 31 by the city's outside counsel, Dixon•Scholl•Carrillo P.A., withdraws the Commission's Motion to Dismiss or in the Alternative Motion for More Definite Statement "in its entirety" and states the city will file a formal Answer to the underlying petition by Friday, Aug. 14.

The case, Chris Edwards v. The Alamogordo City Commission, No. D-1215-CV-2026-00514, was filed June 2 in Otero County district court and assigned to Judge Lori L. Gibson Willard. The petition alleges the Commission violated the Open Meetings Act, NMSA 1978, §§ 10-15-1 to -4, and the Inspection of Public Records Act, NMSA 1978, §§ 14-2-1 to -12, in connection with a series of closed executive sessions concerning the city manager position between March and June of this year.

According to the petition, the Commission voted unanimously, 7-0, on March 10 to direct staff to negotiate a city manager contract with then-Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez. Weeks of closed executive sessions followed. On April 28, within minutes of reconvening from one such session, the Commission voted 4-3 to accept a separation settlement with Hernandez rather than finalize her contract — without public debate nor terms disclosure, the petition alleges a failure to disclose any settlement terms or explaining the reversal in open session.

The city manager position was ultimately filled on June 15, when the Commission voted 5-2 to hire Robert Stockwell following another closed session. The petition contends the actual selection process took place behind closed doors and that the public votes served only to ratify decisions already made in private.

The city has disputed that characterization. In its now-withdrawn motion to dismiss the Commission argued that its charter authority to appoint a city manager permitted it to discuss hiring, departure negotiations, and related settlement matters in closed session under the Open Meetings Act's "limited personnel matters" and "pending litigation" exceptions, and that nothing in the statute required the Commission to disclose candidate names, contract terms, or its reasoning as a part of a public vote.

A motion to dismiss, if granted, can end some or all of a lawsuit's claims before the case proceeds further. By withdrawing its motion, the Commission avoids a ruling on whether the petition's allegations were legally sufficient to proceed — but it also leaves those allegations unresolved, rather than adjudicated in the city's favor.

The withdrawal came 10 days after the court entered a stipulated order granting the city leave to file a sur-reply — a further round of briefing — in support of its motions related to an IPRA. Instead, it withdrew the motion outright for dismissal and the case will now proceed.

The case had been set for a hearing on the motion Aug. 12, 2026. With no motion left pending, Edwards is filing a notice asking the court to vacate that August 12th hearing as moot, or to clarify its purpose if the court intends to use the time for another matter.

Under the city's own notice, an Answer to the petition — the city's formal, paragraph-by-paragraph response admitting or denying each allegation — is due Aug. 14. 

That filing will mark the first point in the case where the city responds to the specific factual allegations in the petition rather than arguing for dismissal on legal grounds.

Separately, a motion asking the court to compel the city's compliance with a pending public-records request — covering city manager candidate scoring materials and other records — has been fully briefed since early July and remains awaiting a ruling.

Alamogordo Town News will continue to report on developments in the case as they occur.

This article is based on filings of public record in the Twelfth Judicial District Court, Otero County. Copies of the referenced filings are available through the Otero County Clerk's office.

item.title: Holloman's Big Give Closes with Celebration at Casa Motors: 19 Teams, Thousands of Volunteer Hours, and a Community That Won Big
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The 2026 Cosa Motos Holloman AFB Big Give Partnership came to a festive close Monday evening as the general manager of Casa Motors hosted a reception honoring the 19 squadron teams from Holloman Air Force Base that fanned out across Alamogordo, Tularosa and Ruidoso over the past month, contributing thousands of volunteer hours to small businesses, nonprofits and community projects across the region.

The Big Give is a month-long initiative in which Holloman squadrons partner with local communities across the Tularosa Basin and beyond to restore and improve public and commercial spaces — service beyond the mission that base officials say strengthens the bond between airmen and the communities they call home. This year's 19 projects ranged from work at the VFW Post 7686 and support for Alamogordo MainStreet to cemetery restoration and water cleanup efforts.

Monday's reception served double duty: the public cast ballots for the People's Choice honors while a voting panel weighed the field to crown the overall champions of an event in which, by every account in the room, the real winner was the community itself.

From Prime Time to the Tularosa Basin: How the Big Give Began

The Big Give tradition at Holloman traces its inspiration to an unlikely source: network television. In 2008, ABC aired “Oprah's Big Give,” a reality series created and produced by Oprah Winfrey through Harpo Productions and hosted by Nate Berkus, in which ten contestants crisscrossed the country competing not to get, but to give — taking on charitable challenges in a different city each week before a panel awarded the final $1 million prize. The show lasted only a single season, but Winfrey's parting challenge outlived it. She urged viewers not to wait for a television crew: rally your friends, your family and your neighbors, she said, and pull off your own Big Give in your own community.

Casa Motors participating with Team Holloman took her up on it. In the years that followed, base leadership and community partners organized the first Casa Motors Big Give, adapting the show's format into a friendly squadron-versus-squadron competition with a distinctly local purpose — pouring airmen's sweat equity into the small businesses, nonprofits and public spaces of Otero County. What began as a television-inspired experiment has grown into one of the most anticipated annual traditions in the base-community relationship: a full month in which squadrons scout projects, adopt organizations in need of a volunteer boost, and compete for bragging rights measured not in dollars raised but in fences painted, exhibits rebuilt, murals completed and hours given.

Nearly two decades on, the format remains true to its origins — teams, projects, judges and awards — but the stakes have inverted from the television version. On the show, one contestant walked away with a million dollars. At Holloman, the prize pool is the community itself, and this year it paid out across three towns: from a fresh mural and refurbished overhang on New York Avenue completed by the 54th Operations Support Squadron in Alamogordo's historic downtown, to cemetery restorations, water cleanups and the transformation of the zoo's bird exhibit.

2026 Big Give Honors

Award

Recipient

Community Choice Award

29th Attack Squadron

Small Team Award

314th Fighter Squadron

Large Team Award

49th Equipment Maintenance Squadron — Alameda Park Zoo bird exhibit

The Large Team Award recognized the 49th Equipment Maintenance Squadron for its major renovation work at the bird exhibit at the Alameda Park Zoo — one of the most ambitious undertakings in this year's slate of projects.

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald told the gathering she was "deeply moved by the level of effort Holloman personnel brought to the community this year, taking on 19 projects that touched everything from the VFW post and Alamogordo MainStreet to local cemeteries and regional water cleanup initiatives."


“The Big Give exemplifies Holloman’s commitment to community, family and mission.”

— Col. Michael S. Mullin, 49th Wing commander

Col. Michael S. Mullin, who assumed command of the 49th Wing on June 4, said he was proud of his airmen's effort and looks forward "to even deeper engagement with the broader Alamogordo and Otero County community." Mullin said the Casa Motors Big Give exemplifies Holloman's mission pillars of community, family and mission — and added that he and his family "love being back in Alamogordo for his second tour at the base."

Mullin knows at least one of this year's winning teams well: he served as director of operations and then commander of the 314th Fighter Squadron — this year's Small Team Award winner — during his first Holloman assignment from 2018 to 2021, before returning this summer from Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, where he was deputy commander of the 354th Fighter Wing.

With thousands  airmen, family members and civilian employees, Holloman's population accounts for more than a third of the Alamogordo area — and events like the Casa Motors Big Give are a visible reminder that the relationship runs in both directions. 

Alamogordo and Holloman were jointly recognized with the Altus Trophy, the Air Force community-support honor, underscoring a partnership both the city and the base continue to invest in.

As the applause faded Monday night and the award winners found their new homes, the scoreboard was clear: 19 teams, three awards, thousands of hours — and one community better for all of it.

item.title: Recent Suicide and Escape Highlight Ongoing Issues at For-Profit Facility Of Lincoln County Jail
item.description:
An inmate who escaped from the Lincoln County Jail has been apprehended, law enforcement officials confirmed. The recapture ended a search that heightened concerns about security at the facility, which is already facing scrutiny over chronic understaffing and inadequate oversight.

Escape and Recapture

Ralph Miranda escaped from the Lincoln County Detention Center but was taken into custody by Lincoln County Sheriff’s Deputies in Carrizozo a short time after his escape.

The rapid apprehension involved a coordinated multi-agency response, according to Sheriff Michael Wood. The following agencies assisted in the capture:

• Carrizozo Police Department

• New Mexico State Police

• Capitan Police Department

• Ruidoso Police Department

Sheriff Wood released a statement thanking all responding agencies for their quick action and coordinated efforts, which resulted in Miranda’s swift recapture and helped ensure community safety.

Two Crises in Days Raise Critical Questions

The escape occurs just days after an inmate died by suicide at the Lincoln County Detention Center—a death that occurred in a cell equipped with video monitoring. The incident has prompted urgent questions about supervision protocols, staff availability, and whether appropriate intervention measures were in place.

The back-to-back crises—the suicide followed by the escape—have intensified community and official scrutiny of operational safety at the facility. Together, these incidents paint a picture of a detention center struggling under operational strain.

“The timing of these two serious incidents is alarming,” said observers monitoring the situation. “When you have a suicide followed by an escape within days, it raises fundamental questions about whether this facility is being properly managed and staffed.”

Broader Context: Systemic Staffing Crisis

The escape incident comes as the Lincoln County Detention Center, operated by private corrections company CSG (Corrections Services Group), faces a critical contract renewal decision scheduled for October. Sheriff Wood has indicated that a full investigation into the escape will be underway and one is ongoing into the suicide per sources within the Department as well. 

However, the escape occurs against a backdrop of more profound operational concerns that have mounted over recent weeks:

Chronic Understaffing and Excessive Overtime: The detention center has been operating significantly understaffed, with correctional officers regularly working excessive overtime shifts. This chronic staffing shortage has persisted despite corrections experts questioning whether current staff levels meet optimal requirements for a facility of this size and inmate population.

Dangerous Medical Support Gaps: Perhaps most critically, there is no nurse or medical personnel stationed at the facility during overnight shifts. This absence of immediate medical response capability raises serious questions about the facility’s ability to respond to inmate medical emergencies—a concern made more acute by last week’s inmate suicide, which occurred in a monitored cell.

Staff Fatigue and Supervision Concerns: 

The excessive overtime required by understaffing has raised concerns among both staff and outside observers about whether tired, overworked officers can maintain adequate supervision and respond appropriately to crises. When a facility is continuously short-handed, the quality of oversight deteriorates.

Suppression of Incident Reporting: Sources with the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Department have alleged that jail leadership has discouraged staff from reporting operational problems and safety concerns to the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, potentially limiting critical oversight by elected officials responsible for the facility. This alleged suppression of reporting raises questions about accountability and transparency.

Public Records Request Seeks Accountability: 

Alamogordo Town News has filed an Information and Public Records Act (IPRA) request seeking documentation on:

• Staffing levels at the time of the recent suicide

• Optimal staffing levels for the facility

• Current inmate census

• Documentation of the suicide incident and staffing conditions

• Issues surrounding the pending contract renewal

October Contract Renewal Becomes Critical

The October contract renewal with CSG now takes on heightened significance. Lincoln County officials—including the Sheriff’s Office and County Commission—will face pressure to address fundamental questions:

• Can CSG adequately manage this facility with current staffing levels?

• What assurances will the company provide regarding medical staffing for overnight shifts?

• How will the county ensure that incident reporting is not suppressed?

• What oversight mechanisms will be put in place to prevent future incidents?

• Should the county consider alternative operators or increased public management?

The renewal decision will effectively signal whether Lincoln County is committed to addressing these critical safety and operational issues or willing to continue under the status quo.

Next Steps

Alamogordo Town News’s IPRA request for incident documentation and staffing records will provide crucial information about whether claims of understaffing and inadequate oversight are borne out by official records. The responses to this public records request will likely shape the contract renewal discussion in October.

item.title: In Memory of Laura Ann Peek
item.description:
Laura Ann Peek passed away at the hospital in El Paso, TX on July 25, 2026. She was born on September 26, 1964, to Thomas L. and Lynne E. Peek in Key West, Florida. She was the oldest daughter of 4 children.

Being a Navy family for 20 years, Laura traveled a lot with us. First home for her was Key West and then on to San Diego, CA for a number of years. After that, on to North Gower, Ontario, Canada for our last duty station. During these travels, we went through lots of places, Washington DC, Texas, Tennessee, Missouri, New York, New Hampshire, and Vermont.

After retiring from military life, we settled for a while on 16 Springs Rd.in NM. Like in Canada, we raised sheep, 2 calves and a garden, which she helped with. We had lots of dogs as pets. We lived in Cloudcroft, NM a short while where Laura finished school at Cloudcroft High School. From there we moved down the mountain to Alamogordo, NM.

Laura was with us till the age of 36. She then moved to a small group home in Las Cruces, NM for 24-hour care. She enjoyed getting out into the community and travel with caregivers to Disneyland, CA, Albuquerque Zoo and museums, and Ruidoso, NM.

Her father Thomas, passed away in 2018. Laura is survived by her sisters, Susan Schexnayder of Arvada, CO and Michelle Collins and husband Dusty of Alamogordo; her brother, Steven Peek of Alamogordo; nephew, Dustin Schexnayder of Wheat Ridge, CO; niece, Casen Collins Fisher and husband Austin of Fitchburg, WI.

Even with Laura's disabilities, she had a full life and many happy memories.

Burial will be held at Monte Vista Cemetery at a later date.

In lieu of flowers, please donate to the Epilepsy Foundation or a charity of your choice.

item.title: Crisis at Lincoln County Correctional Center: A Troubling Pattern Emerges as Private Operator Seeks Contract Renewal
item.description:
A cascade of serious incidents at Lincoln County Detention Center has reignited debate over whether for-profit corporations should be running county jail facilities, raising pressing questions about accountability, oversight, and public safety.

The troubled facility has been beset by a pattern of concerning incidents in recent weeks: a suicide, reports of severe understaffing, an inmate escape, and most damaging of all, allegations of gross misconduct by a compliance officer whose explicit duty was to ensure the jail followed state and federal law.

Yet despite these crises, the for-profit operator running the facility is seeking renewal of its contract with Lincoln County—a development that has sparked outrage among those questioning whether private corrections corporations should hold county jail contracts at all.

A Compliance Officer's Breach of Trust

The most egregious case involves Leticia Amaya, 35, the jail's compliance manager—the very person tasked with ensuring the facility adhered to state and federal regulations, including the federal Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA).

Instead, Amaya allegedly conducted a sexual relationship with an inmate in her custody, becoming pregnant with his child and engaging in sexual encounters in a mop closet and other areas of the jail facility.

Amaya now faces three counts of criminal sexual penetration and one count of tampering with evidence. According to court documents filed in 12th Judicial District Court, the relationship with the inmate occurred roughly between July and September 2025.

While the court records indicate the relationship appeared consensual, PREA explicitly prohibits prison or jail officials from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with inmates—a prohibition Amaya, as compliance manager, was specifically hired to enforce. The very person responsible for holding the jail accountable to federal law became the subject of federal law violations.

Damning Details Emerge

Investigation by the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office revealed the extent of the breach in court records. When the began investigating after learning of the relationship, leaders listened to recorded jail phone calls between Amaya and the inmate.

"It was obvious that the two were in a relationship, as they used terms of endearment," staff leadership told detectives, according to a criminal complaint filed by Detective Bryce Bailey.

The inmate had been held at the facility between May 2025 and September 2025. According to documents, Amaya and the inmate had sexual encounters multiple times, including in a mop closet, a booking area closet, and a vacant cell he was painting.

When confronted with recordings of jail phone calls in which she told the inmate she was pregnant, Amaya initially denied the relationship and falsely claimed the baby belonged to her ex-husband. She eventually admitted the truth: she was pregnant with the inmate's child, had engaged in a "boyfriend and girlfriend" relationship with him while he was incarcerated, and had violated the very federal law she was hired to protect.

Amaya was charged in February 2025 and is currently free on her own recognizance. A trial is scheduled for December.

Broader Pattern of Failure

The Amaya case is not an isolated incident, but rather the most visible manifestation of a troubling pattern at LCDC.

In recent weeks, the facility has experienced:

A suicide that has raised questions about mental health protocols and staffing levels with pending IPRA requests seeking information and details. 

Critical short-staffing that has compromised security and operations

An inmate escape that exposed vulnerabilities in facility management and security procedures

These incidents collectively paint a picture of a facility spinning out of control, with inadequate supervision, insufficient staffing, and a breakdown in the chain of command and institutional accountability.

The Private Prison Debate: Why Should Corporations Run County Jails?

The ongoing crisis at LCDC has renewed a fundamental question: Why are for-profit corporations running county jail facilities instead of locally accountable sheriff's departments?

Unlike public jails operated directly by sheriff's departments, private jail operators have a financial incentive to minimize costs—often at the expense of staffing, training, and oversight. They are accountable to distant corporate headquarters and shareholders, not to the communities they serve.

A county sheriff, by contrast, is directly elected and answers to county voters. A sheriff oversees the jail as part of a broader law enforcement mission, with institutional stability and community accountability built into the governance structure.

"There's an inherent conflict of interest when a corporation profits from incarceration," critics argue. "Cost-cutting directly impacts safety, and when something goes wrong, the corporation can simply decline to renew a contract and move on, leaving the community to pick up the pieces."

Contract Renewal Under a Cloud

Against this backdrop, the private operator's bid for a new contract in Lincoln County raises troubling questions. How can the county justify renewing a contract with a corporation that:

Has lost operational control of the facility, as evidenced by a suicide, an escape, and staffing crises?

Employed a compliance manager who violated the very federal law she was hired to enforce?

Has documented problems with institutional oversight and accountability?

Prioritizes profit margins over adequate staffing and security?

County officials face a critical decision point and citizens must demand answers. Do they continue with a failing private model, or do they consider bringing jail operations back under public control, where accountability runs through elected sheriff leadership rather than corporate management structures?

Questions Without Answers

As Amaya awaits trial, and as LCDC continues to grapple with the fallout from multiple crises, the underlying questions remain unanswered:

Where was the management oversight that should have caught Amaya's relationship before it progressed to pregnancy?

Why was understaffing allowed to reach levels that contributed to a suicide and an escape?

What institutional failures permitted a compliance officer to violate the very federal statutes she was responsible for upholding?

And most fundamentally: Should Lincoln County continue entrusting its jail to a for-profit corporation, or should it demand that a public agency—accountable to voters—manage the facility?

These are not academic questions. They go to the heart of public safety, institutional accountability, and the basic principle that those who deprive people of their liberty must be subject to rigorous public oversight.

As Lincoln County considers the private operator's contract renewal request, the answer to these questions will determine whether the facility can rebuild public trust or whether it continues on its current troubling trajectory.

item.title: Court of Appeals Denies Republican Party’s Final Appeal in Barela Leadership Dispute
item.description:
SANTA FE, N.M. — In what may be the final chapter of a bitter intra-party legal battle, New Mexico’s Court of Appeals has denied the Republican Party of New Mexico’s petition for writ of error on August 5, 2026, effectively upholding the lower court’s controversial decision to remove Amy Barela from her position as state party chairwoman.

The three-judge appellate panel, consisting of Justices Jacqueline R. Medina, J. Miles Hanisee, and Gerald E. Baca, remanded the matter back to Otero County District Court for further proceedings. The order closes a legal chapter that has roiled the state’s Republican Party for months and raised questions about the judiciary’s proper role in resolving internal party disputes.

A Party at War with Itself

The conflict that led to this ruling originated when two separate lawsuits were filed in May 2026 seeking the ouster of state GOP chairwoman Amy Barela, with one filed in Bernalillo County and another in Otero County. The plaintiffs — including lieutenant governor candidate Aubrey Blair Dunn, Otero County Commission candidate Jonathan Emery, gubernatorial candidate Duke Rodriguez, and other party members — argued that Barela had violated party rules by refusing to step aside while simultaneously seeking re-election to her Otero County Commission seat.

The central issue hinged on the Republican Party’s own internal rules. Party rules prohibit chairpersons from holding the post while also running in a contested primary. This conflict-of-interest provision was designed to prevent party leaders from using their official positions to advantage their own candidacies.

The Lower Court’s Dramatic Ruling

On May 27, 2026, Thirteenth Judicial District Judge Cindy Mercer issued a preliminary injunction that prohibits Barela from continuing to serve as chair and also orders party officials not to publicly support any of the Republicans running for office during the ongoing primary.

The injunction came just days before the June 2 primary election and sent shockwaves through Republican circles. Aubrey Blair Dunn, who is running for lieutenant governor as a Republican and was one of the plaintiffs, said the party’s decision to appeal is misguided, stating “The judge’s decision was clear, well-reasoned, and plainly correct, and dragging it into an appeal does nothing but waste the Party’s limited resources and the Court’s valuable time.” Gubernatorial candidate Duke Rodriguez, another plaintiff, said an appeal will only distract from the Republican Party’s efforts to win elections.

The Party’s Appeal and Supreme Court Loss

Undeterred by these comments from fellow Republicans, the party and Barela herself filed an emergency petition to the New Mexico Supreme Court. The Republican Party of New Mexico argued that a lower court judge’s ruling was unprecedented and “extraordinary”.

The New Mexico Supreme Court on June 10, 2026, denied the Republican Party of New Mexico’s appeal of the lower court ruling. The state Republican party filed an emergency petition on May 29, arguing it violated party members’ free speech rights and that courts are not the proper venue to resolve intra-party disputes. The New Mexico Supreme Court unanimously denied that petition without explanation.

That rebuke at the state’s highest court set the stage for today’s appellate court decision, which further demonstrates the judicial system’s determination to enforce the will of the lower court.

Political Consequences and Timing

The legal battle’s impact on the 2026 election cycle was immediate and profound. Amy Barela was ousted from the Otero County Commission by a 46-vote margin in the primary election, just days after a judge ordered her to step down from her party post.

The tight loss raises questions about whether Barela’s legal troubles affected her electoral prospects, or whether she was simply defeated by a well-organized opponent. Jonathan Emery narrowly beat Barela in the June 2 primary election.

A Fractious Party

The dispute reflects deeper divisions within New Mexico’s Republican Party heading into a critical election year. The party has struggled with leadership and message coherence, particularly on statewide races. The internal legal war has consumed resources and attention that many Republicans believe should have been focused on challenging Democratic control of state offices.

The broader context involves questions about presidential loyalties within the state GOP. Though not explicitly stated in court documents, the lawsuit emerged amid broader national Republican tensions between traditional party conservatives and more populist wings.

What Happens Next

With the Court of Appeals having remanded the case back to District Court, the matter is not entirely resolved. The lower court will likely address remaining questions about party governance and potential damages. Additionally, questions remain about how the party will move forward in selecting new leadership.

Earlier this summer, the party was scheduled to name a new chair at a June 20 State Central Committee meeting in Las Cruces, though the full details of that process and whether all leadership questions have been resolved remain unclear.

A Lawyer’s Perspective

Aubrey Blair Dunn, one of the plaintiffs and himself a lawyer serving Albuquerque in Administrative Law and Appeals cases, viewed the case as a straightforward application of existing party rules. The Court of Appeals’ decision appears to validate his interpretation that judges do have a role to play when internal party matters rise to the level of contractual disputes governed by written bylaws and rules.

The ruling also suggests that while courts generally try to avoid interfering in internal party politics, they will intervene when a party’s own written rules have been clearly violated and members take legal action.

Looking Forward

Today’s decision by the Court of Appeals effectively closes one chapter of the Republican Party’s internal warfare, though questions remain about whether this ruling will be the final word or if further legal challenges are possible.

For Barela, the defeat marks a dramatic fall from power for the chairwoman who led the party into 2026. She remains an Otero County resident and her political future remains uncertain.

For the plaintiffs — including Dunn, Emery, and Rodriguez — the wins in court and at the ballot box represent vindication of their position that party rules exist to prevent exactly the kind of conflict-of-interest situation Barela allegedly created.

For the New Mexico Republican Party itself, the question now becomes whether it can move forward unified under new leadership, or whether the bitterness of this legal fight will continue to hamper Republican efforts to regain statewide offices.

item.title: Tiger Territory Ready to Roar: School Returns and Football Season Launches

Back to School Begins Wednesday

The 2026 school year launches with a staggered start designed to give every student their moment:

• Wednesday, August 12: Kindergarten, 6th grade, and 9th grade students report for their first day

• Thursday, August 13: All remaining students return, completing the full enrollment

“This staggered approach allows us to focus on each transition cohort,” said a school official. “We want every student—whether it’s a kindergartener entering school for the first time or a ninth grader stepping into high school—to feel welcomed and supported.”

The district’s commitment to a safe, inclusive environment extends beyond academics.

But Football Waits for No One

Even as the school year officially begins, Tiger football is already in motion. The varsity team takes the field Thursday, August 13 at 4:00 PM for their scrimmage against Carlsbad at Ruidoso Middle School—just hours after students return to class.

The Week That Changes Everything

Consider what happens in Alamogordo next week:

• A kindergartener nervously walks through the doors of Alamogordo Elementary, clutching a new pencil and backpack

item.title: In Memory of Jerry Lynn Guss
