item.title: Letter to the Editor: Tularosa’s Water Crisis Is a Failure of Municipal Choice, Not an "Act of God" By Glenn Bell
item.description:
To the Editor:

Recent reporting on Tularosa’s emergency water ban repeats local government talking points, framing empty tanks and dry lawns as an unavoidable "Act of God." A review of public records, federal disaster declarations, and hydrological data reveals a far different reality: this crisis was entirely manufactured by administrative neglect.

When the South Fork and Salt Fires burned across Otero and Lincoln counties, federal and state emergency managers issued explicit hydrological warnings: post-fire ash, soot, and mud runoff would threaten downstream water intakes during subsequent monsoon cycles. In response, President Biden approved FEMA Disaster Declaration DR-4795, making millions of dollars in Public Assistance and Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) funds available to Otero County and the Village of Tularosa to build pre-settling basins, sediment traps, and alternative water infrastructure.

What did municipal and county leadership do with this window of opportunity? Nothing.

When monsoons inevitably washed ash down Tularosa Creek, the village intake was overwhelmed by mud and forced to shut down. Had leadership deployed federal hazard mitigation dollars over the prior two years, pre-settling filtration would have processed the intake.

Worse still, leadership completely ignored clean water sitting directly above them. Under New Mexico State Engineer policy, rooftop rainwater harvesting is 100% legal and requires no water rights permits. Tularosa’s Approx.15 municipal and school buildings represent roughly 80,000 square feet of roof space. Equipping public facilities and residential homes with simple gutter and cistern catchment systems using available federal resilience funds would have harvested millions of gallons of pristine, ash-free water during monsoon rains—bypassing the contaminated creek entirely.

Compounding this supply-side failure is baseline demand neglect. As early as May 2019, independent testing on Tularosa City Hall’s own lawn proved that biological soil amendments could reduce turf irrigation demand by 33% to 70% while restoring green space. Instead of adopting biological water conservation across 26.6 acres of public grounds to keep municipal tanks full, the village maintained flood-irrigation practices, wasting over 311 million gallons of water.

Under Article II, Sections 4 and 20 of the New Mexico Constitution, citizens have an inalienable right to protect their property, and government cannot inflict uncompensated damage on private property. By choosing not to filter intake water, choosing not to harvest rainwater, and choosing not to manage root-zone water demand, local officials forced an emergency ban that has stripped $12.6 million to $37.9 million in real estate value from Tularosa homeowners while creating a severe wildfire hazard.

Tularosa families are not suffering from a lack of rainfall. They are suffering from a lack of leadership. It is time for the Village Board and County Commissioners to answer for the funding they ignored and the choices that brought our community to its knees.

Glenn Bell

Tularosa, NM

Tularosa Basin Resident & Property Owner

item.title: Remembering A New Mexico Basketball Legend: Coach Frank Edward “Pancho” Dooley
item.description:
Frank Edward Dooley, affectionately known as "Coach Dooley" and "Pancho," passed away peacefully in Albuquerque on August 2, 2026, surrounded by his family. A devoted husband, loving father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, steadfast friend, lifelong athlete, and storied coach and teacher, he leaves a legacy that will endure far beyond his 93 years.

A Life Well-Lived

Frank was born on January 9, 1933, in Deming, New Mexico, to Frank and Evelyn Dooley. He graduated from Deming High School and attended Western New Mexico University in Silver City, where he met and later married his beloved wife, Norma "Jean" Chaudoin. A football player for the Mustangs, Frank was inducted into the Western New Mexico Hall of Fame. After graduating, he served two years in the Army as a Specialist Third Class and received an honorable discharge. Frank went on to earn his master's degree in mathematics from the University of Northern Iowa—a pursuit that reflected his lifelong commitment to education and self-improvement.

Frank and Jean raised their four children—Tim, Bryan, Sandy, and Warren—in Deming, where they built deep and lasting friendships throughout New Mexico. Through decades of shared experiences—countless PB&J sack lunches for basketball road trips, camping adventures along the Gila River, and innumerable New Mexican meals with close friends—Frank and Jean created a family culture centered on care, respect, and community.

A Champion Coach and Beloved Teacher

Frank was a renowned basketball coach and mathematics teacher whose influence shaped thousands of young people over his distinguished 40-year career. With an impressive career record of 446 wins and 215 losses, Coach Dooley became a fixture in New Mexico high school athletics.

He is especially celebrated for his tenure coaching the Deming Wildcats from 1963 to 1979, where he compiled 313 wins and led the team to four State Championships (1971, 1972, 1974, and 1976). Beyond Deming, Coach Dooley had additional coaching stints across New Mexico, including Silver, Alamogordo, Mayfield, St. Pius, and Cibola—communities where he left an indelible mark on young athletes and students.

His excellence was recognized throughout the region and nation: New Mexico Coach of the Year (1971-1972), National Basketball Coach of the Year for the Southwest Region (1972), induction into the New Mexico High School Coaches Hall of Fame (1990), and most recently, the National High School Athletic Coaches Association Hall of Fame (2025). The Deming High School basketball court was officially named "Frank Dooley Court" in 2010, and the school's new gymnasium was named in his honor in 2017—tributes that speak to the profound impact he had on his community.

Alamogordo: Building Champions and Leaders

During his coaching tenure in Alamogordo in the 1980s, Coach Dooley demonstrated the same championship mentality that defined his career. He led his team to a second-place finish at the state championship—a remarkable achievement that showcased his ability to build competitive programs across different schools and communities.

It was in Alamogordo where Coach Dooley's philosophy of holistic student development became particularly evident through his partnership with Coach Bob Sepulveda. Rather than viewing athletic programs in isolation, Dooley actively encouraged his basketball players to participate in Sepulveda's track and field program, understanding that well-rounded athletes and students thrive through diverse experiences.

Coach Sepulveda, whose name now graces Alamogordo's Tiger track and field program, remembered Dooley with deep respect and admiration:

"Coach Dooley was a true mentor who understood that our role went far beyond wins and losses. He was deeply committed to education and to developing rounded student success. He not only coached excellence on the court, but he made sure his players understood the value of pursuing excellence in the classroom and in every aspect of their lives. We worked well together because we shared the same philosophy—that we were building young people, not just athletes."

This collaborative spirit and unwavering commitment to student welfare set Dooley apart. He was respected not merely for his coaching acumen, but for his dedication to the total development of every young person in his care. While Coach Dooley was the head basketball coach and a mathematics teacher he was very supportive of Coach Sepulveda’s and his wife Marylin’s Cross Country teams. He encouraged his athletes to join both Bob and Marylin’s teams, helped with track meets and often socialized with the Sepulveda’s during his tenure in Alamogordo. 

The Teacher Behind the Coach

As a mathematics teacher, Frank brought the same patience, empathy, and intellectual rigor to the classroom that he demonstrated on the court. His students navigated algebra, trigonometry, and calculus under his careful guidance, and many counted him among their favorite teachers. Frank understood that teaching was a sacred trust—that young people needed to feel valued and believed in before they could truly learn.

A Man of Character

Throughout his life, Frank faced challenges on the court, in the classroom, and in his personal journey. He met each with a determined spirit, a positive attitude, and his signature sense of humor. He loved the outdoors—fishing, woodworking, camping—and was known for his strong slices and spins on the tennis court and his fierce competitive spirit in ping pong.

His family remembers his contentment after a "panza llena y corazón contento"—a full belly and happy heart—especially after enjoying spicy chicken sandwiches paired with mocha frappes topped with an extra chocolate drizzle. These simple pleasures reflected the wisdom at the core of his character: that life's greatest riches are found in relationships, good food, laughter, and time spent with those we love.

Just months before his passing, Coach Dooley was honored at The Pit in Albuquerque for the 50th anniversary of his 1976 championship team—a fitting tribute to a coach whose accomplishments spanned decades and whose legacy continued to be celebrated and cherished.

Frank credited his success in coaching to the community around him. He was a true leader who built a culture of care, respect, and discipline wherever he went. His wisdom and goodness live on in everyone who learned from him.

Legacy and Survivors

Frank is survived by his son Tim and his wife Cindy, and their daughters Chantel, Krista, and Tana; his son Bryan and his wife Holly; his daughter Sandy and her husband David, along with their children Laura, Melanie, Staci, Chase, Heather, and Aubrey; and his son Warren and his partner Kris, and their children Stuart, Andy, and Megan, as well as many great-grandchildren. Frank is preceded in death by his parents, his beloved wife Jean, his twin brother Oscar, and his sister Frances.

Honoring His Memory

A private celebration of life will take place for Frank's immediate family. The larger community—the countless students, athletes, colleagues, and friends whose lives he touched—is invited to share memories and stories online and to donate in Frank's memory to the Frank Dooley DHS Scholarship Fund, established in 2013 to benefit Deming High School graduating seniors.

Donations can be sent to:

Coach James Williams

C/O Frank Dooley DHS Scholarship Fund

601 S. Granite St.

Deming, NM 88030

"Whenever you spent time with him, he made you feel like the most important person in the world. He had an infectious love for life and cared for his family and friends. He was the ultimate role model. There are a lot of people that talk but don't walk... he did it all."

Rest easy, Coach. Your legacy lives on in all of us.

item.title: Federal Roadblocks and One Lawmaker's Shameful Attack: New Mexico Epstein Commission Faces Dual Resistance
item.description:
When the New Mexico Survivors' Truth Commission released its interim report on August 5, 2026—phase one of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein's crimes at Zorro Ranch—two forms of obstruction became starkly apparent: political sabotage from within New Mexico, and systematic non-compliance from the federal government.

Rep. John Block, a Republican, wasted no time condemning the work. He called the interim report "feeble," a "nothing-burger," and declared it "helps no victims." He criticized the $750,000 investment as "put into the paper shredder" and cynically asked: "Did we ever think they would hold anyone accountable? I hoped so, but now we have our answer: Nope."

Block's attack studiously avoided mentioning survivors—the women and girls groomed, trafficked, and abused at Zorro Ranch. His criticism was purely fiscal and dismissive, devoid of empathy for victims whose lives were destroyed.

But Block's obstructionism pales beside the federal government's systematic refusal to provide the truth.

The Real Blockade: Federal Agencies Deny Access to Evidence

The interim report was never intended to be final. It is foundational work: organizing 3.5 million pages of documents, issuing subpoenas, identifying witnesses, and establishing investigative procedures. The final report is due December 31, 2026, with extensive depositions and legislative recommendations to follow.

Yet the Commission faces a wall of federal resistance that mirrors the very institutional failures it is investigating.

Of 20 subpoenas issued, only 10 received full compliance. Multiple federal agencies either refused to comply or ignored the Commission's requests entirely:

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), which prosecuted the federal case against Epstein, refused to comply

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida rejected compliance

The Federal Bureau of Investigation has not responded

The Federal Aviation Administration has not responded

JPMorgan Chase, which processed millions in transfers for Epstein, has not responded

U.S. Attorneys' offices in Michigan, South Carolina, and the U.S. Virgin Islands have ignored the Commission's subpoenas

The Epstein Files Transparency Act released 3.5 million of an estimated 6 million pages of documents—but with inconsistent and opaque redactions that obscure critical information. Epstein's emails span only 2009-2019, leaving the 1990s and early 2000s—critical years of his New Mexico operations—undocumented and beyond reach.

This is not accident. This is systematic obstruction by the federal government itself—the very institutions that failed to investigate Epstein's crimes in New Mexico for over three decades.

Block's Constituents Reject His Callousness

The response to Block's attack was swift and unforgiving. One constituent, using the handle "Blockhead," reminded him that the Truth Commission is bipartisan, with "2 of your Republican colleagues" serving—"a former District Attorney & a retired FBI agent" who are "highly respected...not just within RPNM, but across the aisle." The commenter concluded: "You should be ashamed of yourself—just for being you. Stop whining & actually work on something constructive. And support your colleagues."

Another constituent was blunt: "Quit trying to cover for pedophiles."

A third: "What a disgusting representative he is truly deplorable."

Block's position isolated him even within his own party. While 61 of his colleagues, including respected Republicans on the commission, recognize the vital importance of seeking truth, Block prioritized budget criticism over survivors' need for answers.

Institutional Failures Repeated: Federal Obstruction Continues

The obstruction the Commission now faces from federal agencies is itself evidence of the very institutional failures the investigation seeks to document and that Block should be using his position and working to address. The U.S. Attorney for the District of New Mexico (USAO-NM) and the New Mexico Attorney General assumed for years that SDNY would investigate Epstein's New Mexico activities. SDNY never did, focusing instead on crimes in New York, Palm Beach, and the Virgin Islands.

No criminal investigation into Epstein's sex trafficking enterprise in New Mexico was ever opened by federal or state authorities. No search warrants were executed at Zorro Ranch until March 2026—nearly seven years after Epstein's death in August 2019.

Now, when the Truth Commission seeks to finally fill that void, those same federal agencies are refusing to cooperate.

SDNY's refusal to comply with a state subpoena is particularly troubling: they led the federal prosecution of Epstein but apparently have no interest in New Mexico's pursuit of the truth.

A Bipartisan Commission Stands Firm Despite Obstruction

The Truth Commission was established unanimously by House Resolution 1 (HR-1) on February 16, 2026, by a 62-0 vote. This bipartisan support—from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers—reflects a shared commitment that survivors deserve answers and the public deserves to know what happened in their state.

Yet this consensus does not extend to all. Block's criticism, combined with federal non-compliance, represents a coordinated resistance to transparency and accountability.

The message sent is clear: the institutions and elected representatives that failes survivors once are not eager to have that failure documented nor are they outwardly pushing and using their influence to find answers for the victims with empathy and compassion. 

The 7,600-acre Zorro Ranch near Stanley, purchased by Epstein from Governor Bruce King in 1993, became the focal point of what should have been a straightforward investigation. Instead, it has become a window into how institutional obstruction, budget cynicism, and bureaucratic indifference continue to protect secrets at the expense of victims.

What the Interim Report Reveals—And What Remains Blocked

Despite the roadblocks, the interim report documents troubling evidence:

Evidence of abuse occurring at Zorro Ranch beginning at least in 1996. A minor was flown to the ranch at age 15 and sexually molested. Another victim reported being trafficked to the ranch multiple times between 2007 and 2010.

A sophisticated operation supported by multiple enablers: Ghislaine Maxwell, who recruited and groomed victims; Sarah Kellen, who arranged logistics; Brice and Karen Gordon, who managed operations; and numerous employees and contractors who facilitated the enterprise.

Federal and state law enforcement failures spanning three decades. The New Mexico AG opened a criminal review in May 2019 but deferred it to SDNY by July, where it died.

Yet critical evidence remains inaccessible. Banks won't provide full financial records. Federal prosecutors won't release case files. Agencies refuse to respond to subpoenas. Email records exist only from 2009 onward. Half of the estimated 6 million pages of documents remain withheld.

The Final Report Will Tell What Federal Agencies Won't

The Commission's work continues. By December 31, 2026, extensive witness depositions will be conducted. The evidentiary record will be analyzed comprehensively. Institutional failures will be documented. Legislative recommendations will be made.

But this investigation will proceed despite federal obstruction, not because of federal cooperation. Survivors deserve better. The public deserves better.

Rep. Block was wrong and provided an insensitive statement not showing true empathy for the victims: the interim report already helps victims by documenting what happened and establishing that someone in government still believes survivors deserve answers, even if federal agencies have made clear they do not.

The New Mexico Survivors' Truth Commission's full interim report is available at www.nmtruthcommission.com. The Commission continues to seek federal compliance with its subpoenas and welcomes information from survivors and witnesses.

SOURCES & TRANSPARENCY

item.title: Independent Candidate’s Statement on Truth Commission Offers Sharp Rebuke to Rep. Block’s Cynicism
item.description:
Independent Candidate’s Statement on Truth Commission Interim Report Offers Sharp Rebuke to Rep John Block’s Cynicism

The New Mexico Survivors’ Truth Commission faces a wall of obstruction. Federal agencies refuse to comply with lawful subpoenas. Half of an estimated 6 million pages of documents remain withheld. Critical email records span only a decade, leaving decades of Epstein’s New Mexico operations undocumented. Of 20 subpoenas issued by the Commission, only 10 received full compliance.

And from within the state, the criticism comes even more sharply. Rep. John Block called the interim report a “feeble” “nothing-burger” that “helps no victims.” He asked cynically: “Did we ever think they would hold anyone accountable? I hoped so, but now we have our answer: Nope.”

Into this void of obstruction and indifference stepped Grace Nagamine, an independent candidate for New Mexico House District 51

Her statement on the Truth Commission Interim Report  is a direct counter to her opponents dismissal—and it speaks to something Block’s words revealed he does not understand: what survivors actually need.

“The survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes in New Mexico deserve more than silence, more than partial answers, and more than institutional delay,” Nagamine said. “They deserve the full truth.”

Those eleven words capture what Block’s criticism completely missed.

Lived Knowledge of Institutional Failure

Nagamine’s statement carries weight because she does not speak from theory. She comes to the Truth Commission’s work with personal knowledge of what it means to be failed by institutions.

In her book, “Your Neighbor: Living the Fight,” Nagamine details her survival of childhood abuse, domestic violence, homelessness, addiction, and incarceration. She was navigated through Child Protective Services as a parent, the criminal justice system as a defendant, the welfare system as a mother in poverty, and the mental health system while struggling with trauma and addiction.

She did not theorize these failures. She lived them.

That lived experience is precisely what allows her to understand what the Truth Commission is attempting to do—and why federal obstruction of that work is so damaging.

“The pain of abuse is not abstract to me,” Nagamine said in her statement. “I know what it is to live with experiences that others cannot fully understand unless they have walked a similar road. That lived knowledge creates a different kind of urgency—a determination to keep pressing for answers that my opponent has never demonstrated and, frankly, never could.”

That “opponent” is Rep. Block. His opponent is the federal government’s refusal to cooperate. What connects them is indifference.

When Institutions Refuse to Cooperate

The Commission faces federal obstruction at every turn. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), which prosecuted Epstein federally, has refused to comply with the Commission’s subpoena. The Southern District of Florida rejected compliance. The FBI, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase, and multiple other U.S. Attorneys’ offices have simply ignored the Commission’s requests.

This is the same federal government that allowed Epstein to operate in New Mexico for three decades without investigation. It is the same bureaucracy that deferred responsibility between agencies while survivors were being abused.

Now, when the Truth Commission seeks to finally investigate, those same institutions are blocking the path.

Nagamine recognizes what this means. “When institutions that hold critical records refuse or delay, it compounds the original harm,” she said. “Survivors should not have to wait while the powerful or the bureaucratic decide how much truth is convenient to release.”

This is not abstract complaint. This is someone who has lived what happens when systems refuse to cooperate with someone seeking help. She waited in emergency rooms while social workers took hours. She navigated CYFD while caseworkers delayed responses. She fought the court system while judges postponed hearings. She knows the cost of institutional delay.

For survivors at Zorro Ranch, the cost is seven years—from Epstein’s death in 2019 until March 2026 when the first search warrant was finally executed. Seven years of silence while federal agencies decided what to do.

The Truth Commission’s Purpose: Not Prosecution, But Recognition

Block’s criticism that the interim report “helps no victims” reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of what truth commissions do. They are not criminal courts. They do not issue charges or send people to prison. Their function is different and, for many survivors, equally vital: they name what happened, document how it was facilitated, and create an official record that validates survivors’ experiences.

Nagamine understands this because she has lived the alternative: silence, institutional abandonment, and the pain of being told your suffering is not significant enough to warrant investigation.

“The New Mexico Survivors’ Truth Commission was created with a clear and necessary mission,” Nagamine said in her statement. “To investigate what occurred on New Mexico soil, to document the failures that allowed it, and to give survivors a measure of recognition and justice that had been denied for far too long. I trust that mission. I believe in the work the commissioners and special counsel are doing.”

This statement stands in stark contrast to Block’s dismissal. Where Block saw waste and process failure, Nagamine sees purpose. Where Block counted missing charges, Nagamine recognized that recognition itself is a form of justice—the simple act of official investigation that says: what happened to you was real. It matters. We are looking.

For a survivor who has waited decades for someone in government to acknowledge their abuse, that matters more than Block’s cynicism suggests.

Contrasting Responses to Institutional Failure

Block’s criticism of the Commission’s work reveals his approach to institutional failures: he dismisses them as expensive mistakes. He asks why the interim report makes no charges, issues no final findings, offers no immediate recommendations. He counts the cost and declares it waste.

Nagamine’s approach—shaped by her own experience navigating failed systems—is different. She recognizes that change requires persistence, that institutional failure requires documentation, and that survivors require both accountability and recognition.

“I will study its findings carefully and work to turn its recommendations into concrete legislation,” Nagamine said, referring to the Commission’s final report expected in January 2027. “This is not about politics as usual. It is about whether New Mexico will finally choose transparency and justice over continued institutional failure.”

This is not the language of someone looking for quick wins or easy answers. This is the language of someone who has lived long-term institutional resistance and knows that meaningful change requires sustained commitment.

Block has demonstrated no such commitment. His social media attack contained no acknowledgment of survivors, no recognition of the Commission’s work, and no alternative vision for pursuing justice. It was purely fiscal criticism divorced from any survivor-centered framework.

Nagamine’s statement, by contrast, centers survivors throughout. She names them. She honors their pain. She commits to action based on the Commission’s findings.

Federal Obstruction Compounds the Original Harm

The most powerful part of Nagamine’s statement addresses the federal obstruction that is crippling the investigation: “At the same time, I am disappointed by the lack of full cooperation from certain federal authorities and agencies in response to lawful subpoenas. When institutions that hold critical records refuse or delay, it compounds the original harm.”

This sentence shows understanding that goes beyond policy analysis. It recognizes a psychological and moral reality: survivors are harmed not just by the original abuse, but by the institutions that refuse to investigate it.

Every delay, every refusal, every withheld document is a secondary harm that reinforces the message survivors received during their abuse—that their suffering is not important enough to warrant attention.

Federal agencies refusing to comply with lawful subpoenas are not simply being bureaucratically inefficient. They are compounding trauma. They are telling survivors a second time: we will not help you. We will not pursue the truth. We will protect the powerful over your need for answers.

Block does not understand this. His criticism suggests he views the Commission’s work as an optional government expense, something nice to have if it doesn’t cost money or time. He has no framework for understanding why survivors need the Commission’s work.

Nagamine has that framework because she has lived the damage of institutional indifference.

What Representation Looks Like When Led by a Survivor

Nagamine’s final commitment is direct: “When the people of District 51 elect me to represent them, I will treat the Commission’s final report—expected in January 2027—as more than a document to file away. I will study its findings carefully and work to turn its recommendations into concrete legislation that strengthens protections, closes loopholes, improves accountability, and centers the needs of survivors.”

This is not performative. She is not promising to read a report and move on. She is committing to action based on the Commission’s findings.

For a district that includes Holloman Air Force Base, where military families struggle with trauma and separation; where CYFD involvement can traumatize families further; where domestic violence and poverty are endemic, a representative who understands these systems from lived experience offers something different than Block’s dismissal.

It offers the knowledge that change is possible because she has lived it. She survived abuse. She overcame addiction. She navigated homelessness. She rebuilt her life. She founded a nonprofit that now serves families across Otero County. She did not give up when systems failed her. She transformed her survival into service.

That is the kind of persistence the Truth Commission needs—not from survivors themselves, but from their representatives.

The Choice Before New Mexico

The Truth Commission is under siege. Federal agencies are blocking access to records. Rep. Block is dismissing the work as worthless. The investigation faces a final deadline of January 2027, with critical witness depositions and comprehensive analysis still ahead.

In this moment, Grace Nagamine’s statement represents a different choice. It says: survivors matter. The truth matters. Institutional accountability matters. And those of us in government should treat the pursuit of justice as more important than budget criticism or political convenience.

“This is not about politics as usual,” Nagamine said. “It is about whether New Mexico will finally choose transparency and justice over continued institutional failure. The survivors have waited long enough. I intend to stand with them.”

Block asked sarcastically: “Did we ever think they would hold anyone accountable?”

Nagamine is answering: “Yes. And when I’m in office, I will.”

item.title: Deb Haaland and Rep. Vasquez to Attend RECA Film Screening, Host Q&A in Alamogordo
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland and U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez will join director Lois Lipman Wednesday evening at the Flickinger Center for a screening of the award-winning documentary First We Bombed New Mexico, followed by a discussion and audience Q&A.

The event arrives more than a year after Congress finally expanded the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) to include New Mexico’s long-excluded Downwinders — families exposed to radioactive fallout from the world’s first atomic bomb test.

On July 16, 1945, the United States detonated the Trinity device in the desert of what is now the White Sands Missile Range, roughly 40 miles west of Tularosa. Nearby Hispanic, Native American, and other rural communities were never warned. Fallout drifted across the Tularosa Basin and surrounding counties. Residents drank contaminated water and milk, ate local produce and livestock, and raised families in the shadow of the blast. For eight decades they reported elevated rates of rare and aggressive cancers across multiple generations while remaining shut out of the federal compensation program created for other nuclear-test victims.

Tina Cordova, a Tularosa native, cancer survivor, and co-founder of the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium, became the public face of that fight. The documentary, directed by Emmy- and Peabody-winning filmmaker Lois Lipman, follows Cordova’s two-decade campaign of town halls, congressional testimony, and community organizing. Lipman spent roughly a decade documenting the stories of affected families and later re-edited the film after the July 2025 RECA expansion to include the historic breakthrough and its aftermath.

Under the expanded law, New Mexicans who lived in the state for at least one year between September 1944 and November 1962 and later developed one of a list of specified cancers can seek a one-time $100,000 payment. Federal data show that hundreds of claims have already been approved, delivering tens of millions of dollars to New Mexico families, with thousands more applications still pending. Advocates continue to push for further improvements, including higher compensation amounts, additional qualifying illnesses, use of affidavits for older rural and Indigenous claimants who lack complete records, and an extended filing window before the current deadline.

Alamogordo and the broader Tularosa Basin sit at the geographic and emotional center of this history. Wednesday’s screening at the Flickinger Center brings the film, its director, and two of New Mexico’s most prominent elected Democrats to the community most directly shaped by Trinity’s legacy.

item.title: Alamogordo City Commission Meeting Tuesday 630 pm Focuses on Flock Public Safety Technology, School Security, and Sunspot Preservation
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo City Commission will hold its regular meeting Tuesday, August 11, 2026, at 6:30 PM at Donald E. Carroll City Commission Chambers, City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth Street, addressing several key community priorities including public safety technology, school security partnerships, and the preservation of a historic scientific landmark.

Public Comment Opportunities Available

Members of the public wishing to address the commission during the public comment period are required to sign up with City Clerk Rachel Hughs before the meeting begins. Each speaker receives a standard three-minute allocation, though Mayor Sharon McDonald reserves the right to adjust time limits based on the number of public comments received.

The city reminds attendees that the commission chambers are wheelchair accessible. Anyone requiring special accommodations must contact the City Clerk’s Office at 575-439-4100 at least 48 hours in advance.

School Resource Officer Agreement Advances

The commission will consider approval of a Professional Services Contract with Alamogordo Public Schools for three full-time School Resource Officers at the district’s secondary schools during the 2026-2027 academic year. The $138,510.50 contract reflects a cost-sharing arrangement in which the school district reimburses the city for 50 percent of the officers’ salaries and benefits.

According to contract terms, the uniformed officers will provide safety and security services during the school year and perform other law enforcement duties during school breaks. The school district will provide dedicated office space for the SROs at all secondary schools and maintain access to the district’s video surveillance system for law enforcement investigations.

Flock Camera System Delivers Results Per Presentation to Be Discussed 

Police Chief David Kunihiro will present an operational update on the Flock license plate reader and live-view camera system, which reached full installation completion in June 2026. The $500,000, two-year contract approved in February 2025 has equipped the city with 60 surveillance devices.

Crime-Fighting Success: The system has already demonstrated measurable impact on public safety. Hit-and-run crash cases solved increased by 76 percent, with 21 cases resolved in 2024 compared to 37 in 2025. Officers have also used the technology to assist in locating wanted subjects and identifying reckless drivers and suspected impaired drivers.

Specific Case Examples:

In one case, officers quickly determined that a reportedly stolen vehicle was actually undergoing a legal repossession, saving investigative resources and preventing an unnecessary entry into the National Crime Information Center database.

In another investigation, police used Flock data to identify a vehicle matching a description provided by a 78-year-old sexual assault victim. Combined with traditional investigative methods, officers located and apprehended the suspect within 30 minutes, leading to charges of attempted kidnapping, sexual assault, and related offenses.

A third case involved a vehicle theft call at a commercial location. Using vehicle descriptions from witnesses, officers identified a matching vehicle within two minutes through the camera system and determined that suspects were attempting to steal a vehicle while a property owner was defending himself.

How It Works: When criminal activity is reported, officers and dispatchers review available information and search the Flock database using partial license plates or vehicle descriptors. If a match is found, officers review camera footage showing the back of the vehicle, license plate closeup, direction of travel, road location, and time of detection. The system provides fixed-point data only—it does not enable continuous vehicle tracking.

Privacy Protections in Place: All searches require a mandated reason and are subject to monthly audits. License plate reader data is retained for 30 days, while video footage is retained for seven days. Officers must be aware of a crime within seven days to access relevant footage before it expires. The system cannot capture audio, take license plate photos, recognize or identify individuals, or automatically identify crimes.

Sunspot Observatory Preservation Effort

The commission will also consider Resolution 2026-30, which formally requests that the National Science Foundation pause the proposed demolition of Sunspot Observatory and calls on state and national legislators to provide time for exploring development of the facility as a multi-use education and tourism center.

The historic observatory is described as an integral element of the modern history of Alamogordo and Otero County, with significant local and national support for exploring potential development for scientific history preservation, education, and tourism. City Manager Robert Stockwell noted that such development would have a significant positive economic impact on Alamogordo, Cloudcroft, and Otero County.

Meeting Details

The meeting begins at 6:30 PM. Attendees are asked to silence cell phones or set them to vibrate. Those needing to take calls are requested to step outside the commission chambers.

The full agenda, including minutes from the July 28 and July 30 meetings and consent agenda items, is available on the city website at http://ci.alamogordo.nm.us.

item.title: Alamogordo City Commission Moves Forward with 2 Year Flock Camera Contract
item.description:
Two-Year Flock Agreement Brings Advanced Surveillance Technology to Bay Area City

The Alamogordo Police Department has quietly expanded its technological capabilities with the implementation of Flock, an automated license plate reader (LPR) system designed to accelerate criminal investigations and locate suspect vehicles. The $500,000, two-year agreement—initially approved by the city commission in 2024—marks a significant shift in how local law enforcement conducts surveillance, even as it sparks ongoing debate about civil liberties and government overreach.

How It Works

Unlike the continuous tracking systems depicted in crime dramas, Flock operates through a network of fixed cameras positioned at key locations throughout the city. The system captures license plate images and vehicle descriptions of vehicles passing designated points, creating what officials describe as “discrete, timestamped data points” rather than real-time tracking.

“The system acts as a virtual fixed-position officer monitoring key locations 24/7,” according to an internal department overview, helping investigators pinpoint vehicle presence and movement without exhaustive manual surveillance.

Video footage is retained for seven days; license plate data persists for thirty days unless saved as evidence for active investigations. Importantly, the system does not directly provide personal information about vehicle owners—investigators must cross-reference results with other law enforcement databases such as the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) to obtain ownership details.

Results on the Frontline

The APD credits Flock with tangible investigative successes. The system helped improve hit-and-run investigation rates by 76%, according to department statistics. In one case, Flock allowed officers to quickly clear a stolen vehicle report by confirming it had been legally repossessed. In other instances, the system enabled police to locate vehicles matching suspect descriptions within 30 minutes, assisting in the resolution of assault, attempted kidnapping, and shooting cases.

“These stories illustrate how LPR can transform vague leads into actionable intelligence,” the department noted.

Access Controls and Accountability

Department officials emphasize strict safeguards against misuse. Access requires account creation through an administrator; all searches are logged and audited monthly. Internal and software-driven audits are intended to deter unauthorized use—a critical concern given nationwide reports of LPR system abuse by law enforcement agencies.

“Accountability and privacy safeguards are embedded in operational policy,” the overview states, though whether these protections prove sufficient remains contested.

A Patchwork of Surveillance

The Flock system integrates with city-owned cameras and selectively accesses private business cameras—such as those at Lowe’s and Home Depot—when permission is granted. This creates an expanding surveillance network across the city, though many business and private cameras remain beyond official reach, leaving significant gaps in coverage.

Community Concerns Persist

While acknowledging the crime-fighting advantages, some Alamagordo residents have raised concerns about potential mass surveillance, the erosion of civil liberties, and what they view as insufficient public input in the decision-making process.

“Community concerns about surveillance and personal liberty infringement were acknowledged during the approval process,” the department’s summary admits, pointing to broader tensions between public safety and privacy rights that civil liberties advocates argue remain unresolved.

The system’s approval without a community-wide vote has intensified questions about transparency in municipal surveillance decisions, particularly as more California cities adopt similar technologies.

Looking Forward

The Alamogordo Police Department’s LPR implementation reflects a national trend toward automated surveillance tools in law enforcement. As the two-year agreement progresses, the city faces an ongoing challenge: balancing the demonstrable investigative benefits of the technology against legitimate privacy concerns and the need for meaningful community oversight.

Whether Alamogordo will extend the program, expand it, or reconsider its approach remains to be seen—a decision that will likely hinge on the outcome of continued community dialogue and the results of independent audits examining how the system is actually used in practice over the next two years.

item.title: Alamogordo City Commission Unanimously Backs Sunspot Observatory Preservation
item.description:
“This resolution reflects our community’s recognition of Sunspot’s significance to our region and our state,” said Mayor Sharon McDonald, who requested that City Manager Robert Stockwell draft the measure of support. “The observatory is an integral element of Alamogordo and Otero County’s modern history, and we believe there are better paths forward.”

The unanimous passage came after sustained advocacy efforts, including a presentation to the commission by Dave Dooling and other Sunspot supporters in a prior meeting. Dooling and his allies also previously submitted a letter to city officials outlining the case for preservation, urging commissioners to take action.

The resolution emphasizes the potential economic benefits of redeveloping Sunspot for educational and scientific tourism purposes. According to the document, such development could “have a significant positive impact on the economies of Alamogordo, Cloudcroft, and Otero County.”

The City of Alamogordo has joined other stakeholders calling on state and national legislators to explore alternatives to demolition. The resolution positions Alamogordo as a willing partner in any future development of the historic facility, signaling local support for Sunspot’s transformation rather than its destruction.

The unanimous vote demonstrates the breadth of community support for preserving this landmark of scientific heritage.
